sens: Apparition, manifestation visible de quelque chose ou de quelqu'un
Révélation surnaturelle, apparition divine ou céleste
Expérience mystique où Dieu se fait voir et connaître à une personne
G3701.detail:
1. The word primarily designates what appears to the eyes, what becomes visible: a manifestation or a concrete appearance. In Luke 24:23, the women recount that "angels appeared to them" — the word expresses the sudden appearance of these celestial beings.
2. It more often signifies a supernatural vision, a divine or celestial appearance. In Luke 1:22, Zechariah had "a vision in the temple": this was not an ordinary perception, but a manifestation of God. Paul states in Acts 26:19 that he did not resist "the heavenly vision" — an experience where the risen Christ showed Himself to him in an extraordinary way.
3. The word also encompasses all mystical experiences where God reveals Himself: visions and revelations of the Lord. Paul in 2 Corinthians 12:1 speaks of "visions and revelations of the Lord" — supernatural encounters where God spoke to him and manifested Himself in an unforgettable way.
G3701.origine: The word comes from a Greek root designating the action of seeing or looking (root ὄψ-, which also gave ὄψις, "sight, appearance"). It is formed with the suffix -ία which creates abstract nouns. In biblical Hebrew, it often translates מַרְאָה or רָאָה, which also express the idea of seeing and appearing. The word has evolved in late Greek: optasia is a more recent form of the ancient term ὄψις.
G3701.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament according to the provided usages. In Luke, it designates an experience of personal revelation: Zechariah sees a divine vision in the temple, and the women see the angels appear. In Acts, Paul speaks of "the heavenly vision" where he was confronted with the risen Christ — a foundational experience for the apostle. In 2 Corinthians, Paul lists his mystical experiences by speaking of "visions and revelations of the Lord." Each time, the word refers to an irruption of the divine into human experience, either a visible appearance of beings or celestial realities, or a revelation where God manifests Himself to a chosen person.
G3701.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God is not distant or inaccessible: He manifests Himself, He "appears" to those He chooses. Biblical visions are acts of grace where God takes the initiative to reveal Himself and communicate His message. This teaches that faith is not just an abstract belief, but can include a real and transforming encounter with the Lord. Zechariah, the apostles, and Paul all experienced this concrete divine presence, which changed the course of their lives.

sens: Cuit à feu vif, direct ou intense
Préparé par la chaleur du feu (viande, poisson)
G3702.detail:
1. The word "roasted" designates food cooked over direct heat from fire, until well browned or grilled. It is the simplest and oldest method of cooking: food is exposed to flames or embers. In Luke 24:42, the disciples offer the risen Jesus some "roasted" fish, cooked in this manner, which shows that His resurrected body can eat as before.
2. The term applies to any food prepared in this way for eating: fish from the Sea of Galilee was commonly roasted over the fire, a quick and common method for a fishermen's meal. It is an image of simple, authentic food, ready to share.
G3702.origine: The Greek word "optos" comes from a root meaning "to cook" or "to roast." It is related to words that designate heat and cooking. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew "tzali" (צָלִי), which described the Passover roasted over high heat according to Moses' instructions (Exodus 12:8-9): the people of Israel were to eat the lamb "roasted over the fire," not boiled.
G3702.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 24:42, where the risen Jesus eats roasted fish. This detail, unique to Luke, emphasizes that the resurrected body of Jesus is not an immaterial ghost, but a body capable of eating real food. The Passover context also recalls the Exodus Passover, where the lamb was roasted: Jesus, the new Passover lamb, confirms through this act His permanent incarnation and continuity with redeemed humanity.
G3702.portee: This simple word reminds us of a fundamental truth: the resurrection of Jesus is not a return to a purely spiritual state, but the transformation and perfection of the body. A body that can eat, that shares the table with the disciples, is a true body. For the Christian, this affirms that the body is not a prison to flee from, but a reality that God honors and renews.

sens: in such a way that, how
in order that, with a view to (expression of purpose)
so that (expected or obtained result)
G3704.detail:
1. In a primary sense, the word simply expresses the manner or way in which something is done: "how the chief priests and our rulers delivered him" (Luke 24:20) — here, the word means "in what manner." 
2. Its most common meaning in the New Testament is to indicate purpose or intention: one acts "so that" a certain result is achieved. For example, Jesus tells his disciples: "Pray the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest" (Matthew 9:38) — implied, so that the harvest may be gathered. Or again, Herod wants to seek the child Jesus "so that I may come and worship him" (Matthew 2:8), clearly expressing his (false) intention. 
3. Sometimes, the word introduces a result that actually occurs: "I have raised you up... so that my name may be declared in all the earth" (Romans 9:17) — God acted in such a way that this result indeed happens.
G3704.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and combines the idea of direction or a path (as in "where") with that of a purpose. Originally, it was an interrogative adverb or an adverb of manner. Gradually, it took on the value of a conjunction expressing purpose, which aligns well with biblical thought: to act "toward" a goal, "in the direction of" a desired result.
G3704.emploi: The word appears 52 times in the New Testament, mostly in Matthew (15 occurrences), who uses it to express the intentions of Jesus and his opponents. It always introduces a subordinate clause (a secondary phrase) that depends on a main verb: "Send him so that he may come," "Act so that he may be glorified." After certain verbs (of request, exhortation), it expresses what is asked or what is urged to be done: "Pray... so that" (Matthew 9:38, James 5:16). After action verbs, it expresses the objective: "They sought... so that they might kill him" (Matthew 26:59). The word can also be accompanied by a negation: "so as not to show to men" (Matthew 6:18).
G3704.portee: This small word is a key to understanding motivations in the Gospel: why does Jesus act this way? What does he expect? The word calls us to reflect on our own intentions: do we act "so that" God is glorified, or for other reasons? It also helps us see how God works with a clear purpose, directing history toward the fulfillment of his will.

sens: An image, a spectacle perceived by the eyes
A supernatural appearance sent by God
A divine message communicated through an image or scene
G3705.detail:
1. The word first designates what one sees with the eyes: a scene, a spectacle. When Jesus comes down from the mountain after his Transfiguration, he calls "vision" what Peter, James, and John saw, which the other apostles must not speak of until the Resurrection (Matthew 17:9). 
2. The word takes on a deeper meaning: it is an appearance, an image that suddenly appears, often in a spiritual experience. Cornelius sees an angel sent by God in a vision (Acts 10:3), Peter sees animals and hears a voice (Acts 10:19), and Paul receives a call to go to Macedonia (Acts 16:10). 
3. The vision is always a means by which God speaks. Ananias receives a direct order from the Lord in a vision (Acts 9:10). It is an act of God communicating his will or message to a servant through a spiritual image or scene.
G3705.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb « horaô » which means « to see ». It is a noun that designates the result of the action of seeing: what is seen. In Hebrew, the Bible speaks of « hazôn » (prophetic vision) or « mar'eh » (appearance) — words that express how God reveals himself through images that his servants see. The vision is therefore the experience of seeing something of a supernatural order.
G3705.emploi: The word appears 12 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in Acts (10 times) and in Matthew (once). It is particularly in Acts that visions structure the narrative of the expansion of the Church: Ananias sees the Lord sending him to Saul (Acts 9:10), Cornelius receives a visit from an angel (Acts 10:3), Peter sees unclean animals commanded to eat (Acts 10:19 and 11:5), and Paul receives the call to go to Macedonia (Acts 16:9-10). These visions are decisive moments where God guides his disciples. The word can also simply designate what happened as real or imaginary: Peter doubts whether what he experienced is a true vision or reality (Acts 12:9).
G3705.portee: The vision teaches us that God still speaks to his people, not only through direct words but also through images and spiritual experiences that bring them face to face with him. It shows how the disciples had to abandon their prejudices: Peter did not understand the order to eat unclean animals until the vision explained to him that God was going to open salvation to the Gentiles. For the Christian, the vision reminds us that God takes the initiative to reveal and guide, and that he never abandons his servants.

sens: Supernatural manifestation that a person sees in a particular state (sleep, ecstasy, trance)
The external appearance or visible aspect of a thing or person
G3706.detail:
1. A vision is a divine manifestation that God sends to a person to communicate a message or reveal something to them. It is distinguished from a mere thought: one "sees" it really, as if it were present before the eyes. At Pentecost, Peter recalls the promise of the prophet Joel: young men will have visions, meaning they will see spiritual realities that God will show them (Acts 2:17). The apostle John in Revelation 9:17 describes what he sees: a vision of terrifying horses with their riders, a supernatural appearance in response to his prayer. 
2. The appearance designates what one perceives when looking at something or someone: its look, its visual form. In Revelation 4:3, John sees the one who sits on the throne and describes his appearance, that is, what he looks like: he has the appearance of a jasper and sardine stone. It is the immediate visual impression, the way in which the thing manifests itself to the eyes.
G3706.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb ὁράω (horaô), which means « to see, to look ». It is a fundamental verb that expresses the action of perceiving with the eyes. The noun ὅρασις (horasis) thus primarily designates the act of seeing itself, and then by extension what is seen. In Hebrew, this word often translates מַרְאֶה (mare'eh, what is seen, the appearance) and חָזוֹן (chazôn, a divine vision). This kinship shows that both testaments speak of the same reality: the experience of seeing what God reveals.
G3706.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament. In Acts 2:17, it designates the visions promised by God through the prophet Joel: a direct divine communication. In Revelation 9:17, it is again a supernatural vision, an extraordinary manifestation seen by John. In Revelation 4:3, the meaning broadens: it is the aspect or visible appearance of the one sitting on the throne. The usage thus shows a slight progression: from supernatural seeing (communication from God) to simple visual perception (how something presents itself to the eyes). In all cases, it is what imposes itself on the sight, whether it is a heavenly reality or the physical aspect of a person.
G3706.portee: For the believer, this entry reminds us that God can manifest himself in visible and supernatural ways. Visions are not vague dreams or hallucinations: it is God speaking through what we see. At the same time, the use of "aspect" or "appearance" invites us not to stop at what we see: the important thing is not always the surface, but what it reveals. What God shows us — in vision or through created realities — deserves our careful attention.

sens: That which can be seen, perceptible to the eye
Belonging to the material and sensible world, as opposed to the invisible or spiritual
G3707.detail:
1. A visible object or reality is something that can be perceived with the physical eyes, something that can be looked at and confirmed. It is the opposite of the invisible or imperceptible.
2. In the passage from Colossians 1:16, Paul distinguishes between visible things (the material world: the earth, the objects we see) and invisible things (spiritual realities: angels, heavenly powers). The word emphasizes that everything that exists—whether perceptible to the eyes or hidden—was created by Christ and for Christ.
G3707.origine: The word comes from the Greek ὁράω (horao), which means "to see." The adjective ὁρατός thus describes what is made to be seen, what falls under the gaze. It is a simple and direct word that appears only once in the New Testament, in this great affirmation of Christ's creative omnipotence.
G3707.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Colossians 1:16. Paul uses it to remind the Colossians (a community of young believers in danger of drifting toward false spirituality) that Christ is Lord of all that exists: the visible physical world, yes, but also all the invisible heavenly and spiritual realities. By establishing this parallel between the visible and the invisible, Paul affirms that nothing surpasses the authority of the Creator.
G3707.portee: This word helps the Christian not to reduce reality to the visible, to the tangible. It reminds us that the material world we see constitutes only half—only half—of creation. The God we serve is also the Lord of the invisible spiritual realities: the heavenly powers, the dominions, everything that has a true existence even if we do not see it. This expands our faith to make it more complete and robust.

sens: A reaction of intense irritation, indignation in response to something
An intense feeling of dissatisfaction and rage in a person
The vengeance or punishment that results from it
The reaction of the divine character in response to sin and injustice
The consequences, the destructive effects of this divine anger
G3709.detail:
1. Anger is primarily a strong and violent reaction to what hurts, offends, or provokes. It is the indignation that rises when one sees injustice: Jesus looks "with anger" at the Pharisees who refuse to heal on the Sabbath (Mark 3:5), because their hardness revolts him.

2. In humans, it is the feeling of inner rage, that heat that rises in us when we are provoked or humiliated. The Apostle Paul exhorts: "Let everyone be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger" (James 1:19), thus acknowledging that this feeling naturally resides in the human heart.

3. Often, anger translates into an act of punishment, a retaliation: this is why one can speak of God's "anger" as one would speak of the punishment it provokes.

4. When the Bible speaks of God's "anger," it is His active rejection of sin, His just reaction against injustice and rebellion: "The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness" (Romans 1:18). It is not chaotic rage, but a moral opposition of the Holy One against evil.

5. This divine anger has concrete effects: it is "the coming wrath" (Matthew 3:7), the judgment that threatens unrepentant sinners, from which only faith in Christ saves us (Romans 5:9).
G3709.origine: The Greek word ὀργή comes from a root that first evokes a surge, a natural impulse, or an inner disposition. In biblical Hebrew, it primarily translates אַף (literally "nose"—because it is said that anger "rises to someone's nose") and also חָרוֹן and חֵמָה, which all evoke an inner heat, a bubbling. The Greek word is used for any lively and spontaneous reaction, whether human or divine.
G3709.emploi: The word ὀργή (anger) appears more than thirty times in the New Testament, primarily in Paul. In the Gospels, it denotes Jesus' anger against injustice (Mark 3:5) and John the Baptist's warning about the "coming wrath" (Matthew 3:7, Luke 3:7). Especially in Paul, it is a major doctrinal theme: God's anger against sin revealed in Christ, the salvation that delivers us from it through His death (Romans 1:18; 5:9), and the practical exhortation to master our own anger (Ephesians 4:31, Colossians 3:8). Finally, Revelation speaks of God's anger in the last days, poured out on the wicked (Revelation 14:10, 16:19, 19:15). The word nuances its meanings according to the context: personal impulse in humans, divine justice in God.
G3709.portee: For the Christian reader, this word teaches several essential truths. First, that God's anger is not arbitrary, but a just reaction against injustice and sin. Next, that we are all, by nature, exposed to this anger (Ephesians 2:3), unless saved by Christ. Finally, it calls for mastery: mastering one's own anger, as Jesus did, brings us closer to God's holiness.

sens: State of irritation, wrath that seizes someone
Sudden emotion in response to an injustice or offense
Divine indignation against evil and rebellion
G3710.detail:
1. To be angry is to experience a strong irritation, a violent emotion that disturbs the heart. It is what the master feels towards his servant who refuses to forgive (Matthew 18:34), or the king in response to the murderers of his messengers (Matthew 22:7): an immediate and intense reaction.

2. This anger often arises from an offense, a hurtful word, or an unjust refusal. The older brother of the prodigal son "became angry" when he learned that his father welcomed his unworthy brother (Luke 15:28). It is an indignation that springs up in response to what seems unjust or insulting.

3. Anger can also be justified, particularly divine anger. God becomes angry against evil, against idolatry and rebellion (Revelation 11:18). But human anger requires vigilance: Jesus warns that being angry with one's brother is dangerous (Matthew 5:22), and Paul exhorts believers not to let anger lead to sin (Ephesians 4:26).
G3710.origine: The word comes from ὀργή (orgè), which denotes anger, wrath. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament (which the Greeks translated with this word), we find חָרָה (harâh), which literally means "to heat up," and קָצַף (qatzaf), which evokes a strong irritation. These images of heat and bubbling illustrate well what the Bible means by anger: an emotion that rises, that ignites.
G3710.emploi: The verb appears eight times in the New Testament, always to express someone who "becomes angry" or "is irritated." It is most often used in the passive voice (one experiences anger rather than actively exercising it), except in Luke 15:28 where the older brother "became angry." It is found in the Gospels (notably in Matthew and Luke) in accounts of judgment or conflict: the merciless servant (Matthew 18:34), the king punishing the murderers (Matthew 22:7), the master of the house facing refusals of invitation (Luke 14:21). Paul uses it in Ephesians 4:26 to warn: anger itself is not sin, but it must not lead to sin. Revelation uses it to describe divine anger (Revelation 11:18, 12:17), justified and fearsome.
G3710.portee: This word reminds us that anger is a deep, natural emotion, but it requires vigilance. Jesus does not absolutely forbid it, but warns against it: one can be angry without yielding to sin. The key is not to let anger fester in the heart (Ephesians 4:26). This calls each person to examine their own anger: is it just indignation against evil, or wounded self-love? And to seek, like the father of the prodigal son, to overcome anger with mercy.

sens: easily angered
having a hot-tempered and impulsive nature
acting on impulse rather than reflection
G3711.detail:
1. The word describes someone who gets angry quickly and easily, without needing much to explode. It is the trait of one who does not control their temper. In Titus 1:7, Paul requires that the overseer not be "inclined to anger," meaning they should not be someone whose violent reactions are to be feared.
2. More broadly, it is a hot-tempered disposition: the person is passionate, lively, quick to irritate. They allow their emotions to dominate and lead them.
3. This also implies a lack of self-control: one acts on the impulse of the moment rather than through discernment and calm. It is the opposite of the patience and gentleness that should characterize a leader in the Church.
G3711.origine: The word comes from "orgê" (anger), which expresses indignation, fury, irritation. The adjective "orgilos" literally means "belonging to anger, of a hot-tempered nature." It is a quality of temperament, a habitual disposition rather than a fleeting anger. In the Old Testament, the Hebrew word "hémah" (fury, rage) conveys the same idea of vehement anger.
G3711.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament in Titus 1:7. Paul establishes the qualities that an overseer, that is, a church leader, must possess. He lists a series of faults to avoid: arrogance, hot anger, drunkenness, violence, dishonesty. Placing "inclined to anger" among these disqualifications shows that it is a serious flaw in a spiritual leader. An overseer must, on the contrary, be self-controlled and capable of guiding the Church with calm and wisdom.
G3711.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that quick anger is an obstacle to spiritual maturity and service to God. Especially for those who hold responsibility in the Church, self-control and patience are not optional qualities: they are essential. It is a call to examine one's own heart and to ask God for the grace to transform outbursts into gentleness and listening.

sens: length equal to the span of outstretched arms
depth of water measured by a sounding line
G3712.detail:
1. A fathom is a unit of length based on the human body: it corresponds to the distance between the two hands when one raises their arms horizontally. It is an ancient, practical, and universal measure, as every sailor could verify it on their own body.
2. In navigation, a fathom is used to measure the depth of water. When the ship approaches the shore or enters a port, the crew throws a sounding line — a weight attached to a graduated rope measured in fathoms — to check that the depth is sufficient and that the ship will not run aground. In Acts 27:28, during the storm that carries Paul to Rome, the sailors throw the line and first find twenty fathoms of depth, then fifteen: the bottom is dangerously close.
3. The precise mention of the depths — first twenty fathoms, then fifteen — shows the rising danger as the ship approaches the shallows. This maritime detail anchors the narrative in historical reality and enhances the drama of the impending shipwreck.
G3712.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "orégô" which means to stretch, extend. A fathom is literally "what one embraces" or "what one can reach by spreading their arms." It is an anthropometric measure, based on the human body, like the cubit. The Greeks and Romans commonly used it in maritime navigation.
G3712.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:28. It is during Paul's journey to Rome when the ship is caught in a violent storm in the Mediterranean. The sailors, worried about the imminent shipwreck, throw the sounding line to know the depth under the hull. The specific mention of the depths shows the danger increasing as the ship gets closer to the shallows. This maritime detail grounds the narrative in historical reality and heightens the drama of the shipwreck that will follow.
G3712.portee: This passage reminds the reader that God watches over even the material details of our circumstances, including the storms and dangers that seem to overwhelm us. The sounding line that measures the depth symbolizes our need to know the true depth of our trials — and the certainty that God measures every detail. For the believer in crisis, this narrative invites trust: even in the midst of the storm, even when the bottom is approaching, God does not abandon us.

sens: to reach out for something, to stretch to grasp it
to strive to attain, possess, or reach something
to desire eagerly, to covet, to seek ardently
G3713.detail:
1. In the literal sense, the verb evokes the gesture of reaching out or stretching to reach something: one thinks of someone extending their arm to grasp an object. This is the basic image of the word in ancient Greek.
2. In a figurative sense, "to aspire to" means to seek to attain, to obtain, to conquer something that attracts us. In 1 Timothy 3:1, the word describes one who "aspires to the office of overseer": they stretch all their efforts toward this goal, actively seeking it.
3. Finally, the verb can express a fervent desire, a covetousness. In 1 Timothy 6:10, the expression "possessed by" the love of money shows how this passion seizes and dominates us; in Hebrews 11:16, the ancients "desire" a heavenly homeland, meaning they deeply thirst for it.
G3713.origine: The verb comes from a root meaning "to stretch" or "to extend." The same family is found in words that speak of extension, movement forward. The initial image is very concrete: that of the hand or arm reaching out. The Greek word also translated in the Old Testament Greek (the Septuagint) expressions of ardent desire or seeking.
G3713.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament, always in letters addressed to churches. In 1 Timothy 3:1, it qualifies the legitimate desire to serve as a church leader. In 1 Timothy 6:10, it describes the covetousness for money, which becomes a destructive passion. In Hebrews 11:16, it expresses the deep desire of the ancient believers for their heavenly homeland. In all cases, the word suggests a voluntary effort, an active search, often inward and spiritual.
G3713.portee: This word invites the believer to examine their deep aspirations: what am I truly pursuing? Toward what am I extending my efforts? The Bible uses it to value the aspiration to service (1 Timothy 3:1) and the thirst for God, but also to warn us against the covetousness that diverts us from faith (1 Timothy 6:10). It reminds us that our inner aspirations reveal our true spiritual priorities.

sens: covered with mountains, rugged
mountainous region, hilly terrain
G3714.detail:
1. The word describes terrain characterized by the presence of mountains or hills. It is the adjective formed from the root meaning "mountain": an oreinos country is a land where mountains dominate the landscape. In Luke 1:39, Mary goes "to the mountains," meaning to the mountainous region of Judea where Elizabeth lived.
2. By extension, the word designates the mountainous region itself, particularly when mentioned as an inhabited whole. In Luke 1:65, "in all the mountains of Judea" means "in the entire mountainous region of Judea," that is, everywhere there were inhabitants scattered across these heights.
G3714.origine: The word comes from the root ὄρος ("mountain"). It is an adjective formed regularly to describe what belongs to the mountain, what is of a mountainous nature. In Greek, it was common to form adjectives this way to indicate a quality or a geographical domain. This word often translates the Hebrew הַר (har), the Hebrew word for "mountain."
G3714.emploi: The adjective oreinos appears twice in the New Testament, both in the Gospel of Luke, in chapters 1:39 and 1:65. It is used each time to describe the mountains of Judea, the region where the beginning of the story of John the Baptist and Jesus took place. The context is that of Elizabeth's motherhood and the announced birth of John the Baptist: the mountainous region of Judea is first the place of Mary's journey, then the place where the wonderful news of what had happened spread. The word emphasizes the geography of the territory where these events unfold.
G3714.portee: This word reminds us that the incarnation of Christ and its forerunners took place in a concrete and real geography. The mountainous Judea is not an abstract backdrop, but a rugged, hard-to-access land where the news of grace spreads from one mountaineer to another. This anchors faith in historical and geographical reality.

sens: Longing, thirst for something
Physical or sensual attraction
Passionate covetousness
G3715.detail:
1. Desire is primarily the general longing to have or experience something, a kind of thirst that drives toward an object. It is the appetite of the soul, comparable to the hunger of the body.

2. In a physical and carnal context, this desire can become an intense attraction of the senses, particularly sexual. Paul in Romans 1:27 speaks of men inflamed in their "desires" for one another, describing a disordered passion that drives them to acts against nature.

3. The word can also designate passionate covetousness that seizes someone, this fervor that consumes and causes a loss of self-control — the desire that is no longer a simple wish, but a fire that burns.
G3715.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to stretch toward," "to reach out." It is the image of one who leans forward, standing on tiptoes to reach something. This image of the body in motion well expresses how desire pushes us, puts us in tension toward what we want. In ancient Greek texts, the word designates all types of desires, from the most trivial to the most disordered.
G3715.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 1:27, where Paul describes the dazzlement of humans in the face of idols and the ensuing moral decay. Specifically, he speaks of men inflamed with carnal desire for one another. The context shows a desire that is no longer natural or ordered, but passionate and idolatrous — a manifestation of rebellion against God. Paul uses this word to describe how humanity, turned away from its Creator, allows itself to be consumed by covetousness that dominates and destroys them.
G3715.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that desire in itself is not sin, but its disorder becomes a destructive power. Paul shows that when humanity abandons God, their desires become masters that enslave and dishonor them. Understanding this word helps to see how the grace of Christ must renew our desires: not to extinguish them, but to redirect them toward God and toward what is right and pure.

sens: To move in a straight line, without deviation or detour
Figuratively: to act with integrity and coherence, to live according to just principles without contradicting them
G3716.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to walk straight means to move without deviating from one's path, as one would on a well-marked road. It is the image of a confident and direct gait.

2. Paul uses it figuratively in Galatians 2:14 to reproach Peter for not living "straight" according to the Gospel: Peter claimed to believe in Christian freedom in Christ, but he acted as if he still had to respect Jewish rules to please other Jews. There was a contradiction between his faith and his conduct. "Walking straight" thus means being honest with one's convictions, not contradicting by one's actions what one professes with one's words.
G3716.origine: The word is composed of two Greek elements: "ortho" (straight, correct) and "pous" (foot, walk). The image is that of the foot going straight, without zigzagging. It is a classical word that literally meant "to go straight"; Paul uses it in a moral and spiritual sense.
G3716.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Galatians 2:14. Paul uses it in a decisive moment: he reports how he had to publicly confront Peter because he was not "walking straight" according to the truth of the Gospel. It is a context of fraternal correction on a matter of Christian coherence, where walking straight means refusing compromise and double standards.
G3716.portee: This word calls the Christian reader to integrity: saying yes to Christ must be evident in our actions, not just in our words. It is a call to sincerity and courage to live without contradiction, without adapting our convictions according to circumstances or social pressure. True faith walks straight, with our whole being.

sens: Standing upright, without leaning or bending
Going in a straight line, without detour
Figuratively: conforming to rectitude, to justice
G3717.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is physical: "right" describes a vertical posture, something that stands without bending. In Acts 14:10, a man lame from birth stands "right on his feet" — it is the opposite movement of paralysis, the complete straightening of the body.
2. A path, a line can be "right," meaning without detour, direct. In Hebrews 12:13, the "straight paths" refer to a way that does not stray, leading straight to the goal, as opposed to a winding path.
3. By figurative extension, "rightness" becomes moral and spiritual: a straight path is a life in accordance with God's will, honest and just. The word evokes the idea of not turning away from what is good, of walking without wavering or straying.
G3717.origine: The Greek word "orthos" comes from a root that expresses the idea of standing upright, not bending. It corresponds in Hebrew to the word "yashar," which also means "right" or "just." This family of words is ancient and very frequent in the Bible to speak of what is aligned, vertical, or morally correct. The French word "orthodoxe" (literally "right opinion") comes directly from it.
G3717.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Greek New Testament, always in a concrete or quasi-concrete nuance. In Acts 14:10, it describes the immediate and physical straightening of the lame man, a manifest miracle. In Hebrews 12:13, it shifts to the figurative: believers are urged to follow "straight paths" so that those who falter along the way do not fall but are strengthened. In both cases, the word combines the idea of firmness, stability, and absence of deviation.
G3717.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that faith produces a visible transformation: the lame man stands "right," healed and restored. It also invites to moral and spiritual uprightness — walking on straight paths means living in harmony with God's will, without detour or compromise. It is an exhortation to coherence and stability in the Christian life.

sens: To trace or dig a straight path, without detours
To treat or administer something with fairness and correctness
To present, communicate the word of God without distorting it, in a straight line
G3718.detail:
1. The literal meaning of the word evokes the action of digging or tracing a direct road, without twists: it is the image of a straight line cut sharply into the ground. This is how the word appears in the Greek translations of Proverbs, where it describes the ways of the Lord (Proverbs 3:6).

2. By extension, the verb means "to treat" or "to administer" something in a just and direct manner, without detours or compromises. It is to apply things with correctness, without mixture or confusion.

3. In 2 Timothy 2:15, Paul uses it to describe how Timothy should present "the word of truth": like a worker who rightly divides what is entrusted to him, that is, without twisting it, mixing it with falsehood, or presenting it crookedly. It is to communicate the Gospel with integrity and clarity.
G3718.origine: The Greek word combines two elements: "orthos" (straight, direct) and "temnō" (to cut, to slice). The basic image is that of someone cutting in a straight line, without deviation. It appears in the Greek texts of the Old Testament to render the Hebrew "yashar" (to be straight, correct). The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Paul.
G3718.emploi: This verb is extremely rare in the Bible: it occurs only once in 2 Timothy 2:15, where Paul encourages Timothy to "rightly divide the word of truth." Timothy, as a pastor and teacher, must present the Gospel faithfully and without distortion. The context shows that it is about fulfilling his task with integrity, as "a worker who does not need to be ashamed." It is an exhortation to rigor in the service of the Word: not to twist it, not to take away or add to it, but to transmit it as it is.
G3718.portee: This word reminds the Christian of a serious responsibility: whoever teaches, speaks of God, or witnesses must do so with uprightness and faithfulness. It is not just about speaking the truth; it is about speaking the truth without compromise, without distortion, without mixture. For everyone, the call is to handle the Word of God with respect and correctness, as a steward of a truth that does not belong to me.

sens: To wake up early, at dawn, before day
To come somewhere early, in the morning, for an action
G3719.detail:
1. The verb expresses the action of getting up early, before sunrise or in the early morning. It is the opposite of staying in bed for a long time. The starting image comes from the word "dawn" (ὄρθρος), that particular moment when night ends and day begins.
2. In biblical usage, it means not only to rise early but also to go or come somewhere early in the morning to do something. In Luke 21:38, all the people rose early to come to the temple and listen to Jesus: it is a voluntary, sustained act that shows eagerness and diligence.
G3719.origine: The word comes from the Greek ὄρθρος (orthros), which designates dawn, the moment when night ends. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew "to rise early" (שָׁכַם in the causative form), the characteristic expression of those who act without delay, full of zeal. This verb belongs to the family of words related to the first rays of day and promptness to action.
G3719.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 21:38. In this passage, it describes the behavior of the crowd that came to the temple early in the morning to hear Jesus teach. The context shows that this was not an isolated action but a daily habit of this people animated by a real hunger for listening. The usage emphasizes the regularity, eagerness, and devotion of these listeners who sacrificed their rest to be present in the early hours of the day.
G3719.portee: This word reminds the believer of the importance of diligence and spiritual eagerness. Rising early to seek Jesus expresses a heart that places meeting with God before its own comforts. It is a discreet call not to delay our search for God, to give Him priority at the beginning of each day, with the same fervor as that crowd in the temple.

sens: That occurs at the moment when day is just beginning
Characterizing dawn, the break of day
G3720.detail:
1. This word describes what happens or is done in the early morning, when dawn is just beginning. In Luke 24:22, the women went to the tomb "early in the morning": they went at the moment when day was beginning to appear, before the sun was really up. It is a time of silence and freshness, just after the night.
2. The word evokes the image of dawn and the moment when light is born on the horizon. It is a time rich with biblical meaning: often, it is in the morning that God acts, that important events unfold. Here, the resurrection of Jesus is discovered at this sacred moment of the day.
G3720.origine: The word comes from "orthros" (ὄρθρος), which means "dawn" or "morning" in the strict sense of the moment when night ends. It is a later form of Greek; "orthrinos" appears where an older Greek would have said "orthrios." This root also appears in other Greek words related to morning and dawn. In translating the Old Testament into Greek, this word often renders the Hebrew "shakam" (שָׁכַם), which means "to rise early, to rise in the morning": it expresses this characteristic action of the morning.
G3720.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 24:22, in the account of the Resurrection. The disciples speak to the two pilgrims from Emmaus about the women who went to the tomb "early in the morning." This early moment of the day underscores the importance of this event: the women did not wait for daylight to go seek Jesus; they rose early, in almost complete darkness. It is a concrete detail that reinforces the realism of the account and the fervor of the women.
G3720.portee: This word reminds us that great acts of God often occur at dawn, at the moment of transition between darkness and light. The women who go "early in the morning" to the tomb testify to a living faith, a promptness to seek Jesus. For the Christian reader, this invites a spiritual attentiveness: to be vigilant, to rise early to meet the Lord, as these women do on that resurrection morning.

sens: Dawn, the moment when day begins to break
The early hour, very early in the morning
A moment of renewal or hope
G3722.detail:
1. Morning refers to dawn or daybreak, when light begins to appear on the horizon. It is the precise moment of transition between night and day. In Luke 24:1, the women come "very early in the morning" to the tomb: they arrive at the moment when the sun rises, to carry out their act of mourning.
2. Morning is also the early hour in general, the very early moment of the day. In John 8:2, Jesus arrives at the temple "early in the morning": he then sits down to teach the crowd. Similarly, in Acts 5:21, the apostles enter the temple "early in the morning" to teach there: it is an action undertaken early, before the day is well underway.
3. Figuratively, morning evokes renewal or new hope: just as each dawn follows the night, morning symbolizes a new beginning, a new grace after darkness.
G3722.origine: The Greek word "orthros" literally means dawn, the moment when light begins. It comes from an ancient root related to the idea of rising or emerging. When translating the Old Testament into Greek, the Greek translators used this word for the Hebrew words "shachar" (dawn) and "boqer" (morning), which convey exactly the same reality: the beginning of the day and the renewal of the world at each dawn.
G3722.emploi: This word appears three times in the New Testament, always to mark an action undertaken very early in the morning. In Luke 24:1, the women go to the tomb "very early in the morning" after the resurrection of Jesus — this emphasizes their eagerness and early devotion. In John 8:2, Jesus arrives "early in the morning" at the temple to teach: the choice of morning shows his regular and constant commitment to the work of teaching. In Acts 5:21, the apostles enter the temple "early in the morning" despite their imprisonment the day before: it is an act of courage and faithfulness carried out without delay. Each time, morning marks a moment of beginning, zeal, and action undertaken in the dawning light of day.
G3722.portee: Morning in the Bible is always a time of new grace and renewed faithfulness. When disciples or apostles act "in the morning", it is because they respond promptly to the Lord's call, as soon as the light returns. For the reader, morning evokes this readiness of heart to rise early to seek Jesus, to pray, to serve: it is the image of one who does not wait, who does not postpone until tomorrow, but who turns to God at dawn.

sens: In a correct, just, accurate manner
With propriety and clarity (in speaking)
With sound judgment
G3723.detail: 1. The word describes an action or word that conforms to what it should be, without defect or error. Mark 7:35 uses it for the deaf-mute man whose tongue "was loosed, and he spoke very well" — his words now came out correctly, without hindrance. 2. It also qualifies a response or judgment that hits the heart of the matter. Luke 7:43: Simon the Pharisee has "judged well" in recognizing that the one to whom God has forgiven much must love more; this is the right response. 3. Similarly, Luke 10:28: "You have answered well" means that the lawyer has understood and correctly stated the essence of the Law — to love God and neighbor. The word emphasizes not only the absence of error but a certain excellence or propriety in execution.
G3723.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek orthós (ὀρθός), which literally means "right, straight", hence the image of what is in good order, aligned, correct. It is found in French words like "orthodox" (the right doctrine) or "orthography" (correct writing). In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the idea is similar to yāšār (יָשָׁר), which means straight and just. It is a simple and common adverb that expresses the general idea of rectitude.
G3723.emploi: The adverb appears four times in the Gospels, always in Luke or Mark. It first characterizes a well-executed physical action (the clear speech of the healed deaf-mute, Mark 7:35). It then qualifies a moral and spiritual judgment: Simon rightly recognizes the degrees of divine forgiveness (Luke 7:43), the lawyer faithfully presents the double law of love (Luke 10:28), and the Sanhedrin's messengers give to God what is God's, that is, they recognize His kingship (Luke 20:21). Each time, the word signals a correct understanding and a word that reaches the truth.
G3723.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us of the importance of correctness — in understanding the Word, in moral judgment, and in responding to the message of Jesus. It invites us to listen to words that "speak well", that is, that say just what is needed, and to recognize when someone has grasped the heart of the Gospel. It is a word of divine approval: Jesus says "well" to the one who has understood.

sens: To trace, mark the limits of something
To decide in advance, to fix a resolution
To establish someone in a position or function
G3724.detail:
1. To determine primarily means to trace a limit or boundary: the word comes from a root that evokes the marking of boundaries. This concrete image is found when talking about fixing the limits of land or the borders of a region (Acts 17:26).

2. The word then expresses the idea of making a decision that is imposed in advance, of fixing something irrevocably. This is why it is used for divine or human decrees that define what will happen: "what is determined" (Luke 22:22) or "according to the predetermined plan" (Acts 2:23) speak of an established will in advance.

3. The verb also means to establish or designate someone for a task or dignity: Jesus has been "appointed judge of the living and the dead" (Acts 10:42) — he is officially assigned this role.
G3724.origine: The Greek word horizō comes from a root that designates the tracing of a line or limit (this same root is found in the French word "horizon"). The transition from the concrete sense (tracing a boundary) to the abstract sense (deciding in advance) is natural: to trace a limit is already to fix and determine. In Hebrew, there were analogous words expressing the idea of placing a boundary or establishing a decree.
G3724.emploi: The verb horizō appears eight times in the New Testament, almost always in Luke and Acts, and is used in three main contexts. First, it designates irrevocable divine decisions: God's decree concerning the death of the Son of Man (Luke 22:22, Acts 2:23), the limitation of empires and times (Acts 17:26), or the institution of the day of judgment (Acts 17:31). Next, it speaks of establishing someone in an official function: Christ "appointed judge" (Acts 10:42) or Christ "declared Son of God" (Romans 1:4). Finally, it can express a collective resolution: the disciples "resolved to send" aid (Acts 11:29). Each time, the idea of a firm and irrevocable decision prevails.
G3724.portee: This word invites reflection on the sovereignty of God: nothing takes God by surprise, for everything is known in advance and determined according to His purpose. At the same time, the verb also applies to human decisions (those of the disciples), reminding us that we are called to make resolutions ourselves and to commit firmly. It is a call to faith in divine providence and to the responsibility of our choices.

sens: The geographical area of a city or a people, its boundaries
The land or country where inhabitants live
The land recognized as belonging to a community
G3725.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the extent of land that belongs to a city or region — like the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali where Jesus came to settle (Matthew 4:13). It is the space recognized as under the authority of a people: Herod massacres all the children "in all his territory" (Matthew 2:16), showing that it is the land he governs.
2. By extension, it refers to the inhabited country or land, with its own characteristics — when it is said that a woman "came from those regions" (Matthew 15:22), it designates the country from which she comes. The word can thus apply to an ethnic or geographical region without emphasizing administration.
3. In the Gospels, the word is mainly used to mark a limit, a border that is crossed: Jesus "leaves the territory of Galilee and goes into the territory of Judea" (Matthew 19:1). The idea of passing from one region to another is often present.
G3725.origine: The word comes from the Greek ὅρος (horos), which means "limit" or "boundary." Horion is etymologically "that which has a schedule" — that is, "that which has limits." The plural ὅρια (horia) is commonly used for "regions" or "countries." In Hebrew, the word it generally translates is גְּבוּל (gəbûl), which has the same meaning of "limit" or "border of a territory."
G3725.emploi: The word horion appears 11 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the Gospels (especially Matthew and Mark) and once in Acts. It is often used to describe the movements of Jesus: he arrives "in the territory of Zebulun" (Matthew 4:13), he goes "into the regions" of the coasts of Tyre and Sidon (Mark 7:24, 31), he travels "in the territory of Judea beyond the Jordan" (Matthew 19:1). The emphasis is generally geographical: an event, a character, or a movement is localized. In Mark 5:17 and Matthew 8:34, the inhabitants plead with Jesus to leave "their territory," expressing the idea of possession or local jurisdiction.
G3725.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus' action unfolds in real space, in concrete regions with their boundaries and inhabitants. It invites the reader not to forget the geographical grounding of the Gospel — Jesus is not an abstract character, but someone who travels, who crosses territories, who meets different peoples. It is also a call to grasp that the Gospel gradually extends from one territory to another, to the ends of the known world.

sens: To make someone take an oath
To urgently plead by invoking a sacred authority
G3726.detail:
1. To make someone take an oath: the word refers to the action of compelling someone to swear, to give their solemn word. It is to bind by a sacred promise. For example: in Acts 19:13, the Jewish exorcists seek to make swear by the name of the Lord Jesus to command the evil spirits.
2. To urgently plead by invoking a sacred authority: more broadly, "to conjure" means to plead insistently, to implore with emphasis by appealing to something sacred or powerful. In Mark 5:7, the demoniac urgently pleads with Jesus in the name of God: "I implore you by God, do not torment me" — here, the invocation of the divine name makes the prayer sacred and imperative.
G3726.origine: The word comes from the Greek root ὅρκος (horkos), which means "oath" or "that which binds by an oath." The form ὁρκίζω (horkizō) is the verb formed from this root: it literally means "to bring into the oath" or "to bind by an oath." In the Greek Old Testament, this verb often translates the Hebrew שָׁבַע (shabaʿ) in the causative form, which means "to make swear." The word thus evokes the idea of a sacred chain that binds the speaker to the listener: the oath is a force.
G3726.emploi: The verb "to conjure" appears twice in the New Testament. In Mark 5:7, the demoniac pleads with Jesus "in the name of God" — he resorts to a solemn and sacred form of supplication, as if invoking the divine name to stop Jesus. In Acts 19:13, the Jewish exorcists try to use the same procedure: they seek to "conjure" the evil spirits "by Jesus," invoking the name of the Lord as a force that binds and commands. In both cases, the verb expresses an imperative supplication, a prayer that relies on a sacred power to be heard and obtained.
G3726.portee: This word shows the power of the sacred name and invocation in prayer. When someone conjures, they do not ask politely: they plead with the authority of a promise or a power they invoke. For the Christian, this reminds us that praying is not weak or timid, but is relying on the power and authority of God or Christ. It is also a call to sincerity: one can only conjure in truth, for one invokes the sacred.

sens: Solemn promise made by invoking God as a witness
Commitment pronounced or sworn before witnesses
Act of swearing, taking God as a witness to what one affirms
Sacred obligation one binds oneself to respect
G3727.detail:
1. An oath is a particularly solemn promise, made by putting God forward as a witness and guarantor: the one who swears engages their conscience and responsibility before God. In Matthew 14:7, Herod promises "with an oath" to the daughter of Herodias to give her whatever she asks — it is a public and binding commitment.
2. The oath is also the very act of swearing, the commitment that one pronounces and must keep: "you shall not bear false witness, but you shall fulfill before the Lord what you have declared by oath" (Matthew 5:33), meaning one must not violate the promise made under oath.
3. The oath can also refer to the sworn words, what has been said under oath: in Matthew 26:72, Peter denies Jesus "with an oath," denying that he knew this man — here, the oath is the word spoken to confirm a lie.
4. The value of an oath rests on the one invoked as a witness: in Hebrews 6:16-17, the epistle reminds us that "for men, swearing by a greater is a confirmation that ends all debate; likewise, God, wanting to show more abundantly to the heirs of the promise the immutability of His purpose, has committed Himself by an oath" — God's oath is infinitely stronger than a human oath.
G3727.origine: The Greek word horkos comes from a root that designates the act of binding, engaging, putting under obligation. In Hebrew, the Bible mainly speaks of shéva (שְׁבוּעָה), which comes from the verb shava (שׁבע), "to swear," literally "to enter into an oath by seven" — the number seven symbolizing completeness and solemnity. The oath was a common practice in Israel to confirm a commitment or word, as for covenants with God.
G3727.emploi: The word appears ten times in the New Testament, especially in the Gospels and in the epistle to the Hebrews. Matthew uses it extensively: in the Sermon on the Mount (5:33), speaking of Herod's oath to the daughter of Herodias (14:7, 14:9), and when Peter denies Jesus (26:72). Mark reports the same incident of Herod's oath (6:26). Luke mentions the oath made by God to Abraham (1:73), a covenant oath, and the one God makes to David (Acts 2:30). Hebrews 6:16-17 develops the theology of the divine oath as an unshakeable guarantee of the promise. James warns against oaths, recommending simplicity of speech (5:12). Through these uses, the oath transitions from the human oath (promise made by men) to the divine oath (commitment of God that cannot fail).
G3727.portee: Understanding the biblical oath helps the believer grasp the absolute reliability of God: His promises are not empty words, they are sworn and immutable (Hebrews 6:17). This gives a deep assurance to the heart of the Christian who relies on God. On the other hand, Jesus and James invite a great sobriety in the use of human oaths (Matthew 5:33-37, James 5:12), for only simple and honest words should suffice — it is a call to integrity rather than making promises relying on God as guarantor.

sens: Solemn commitment made by invoking God as a witness
Act of swearing, solemn promise sealed by the name of God
G3728.detail: 1. An oath is a promise made solemnly by taking God as a witness. It is a commitment strengthened by the invocation of the divine name, which makes it irrevocable and sacred. In Hebrews 7:20-21, the text emphasizes that Jesus was appointed as a priest "with an oath" — which reinforces his authority and eternal character, unlike the Levitical priests who were not appointed with such an oath. 2. In biblical language, an oath is the act of swearing, the assurance given solemnly. In Hebrews 7:28, "the word of the oath which was made after the law" shows that the divine oath concerning Jesus is an absolute guarantee — God himself commits, which is stronger than any human law or institution.
G3728.origine: The Greek word comes from two roots: "horkos" (oath) and "omnymi" (to swear, to bind oneself by a solemn promise). It literally designates the affirmation made under oath, the act of taking God's name as a witness. It is a compound word that marks the seriousness of the bond contracted between the one who swears and God.
G3728.emploi: The word appears three times, only in Hebrews, chapter 7, in a fundamental passage on the priesthood of Christ. The author of the epistle builds his argument in contrast: the Levitical priests were appointed without an oath (it is a mere legal institution), but Jesus was appointed as a priest with a divine oath (Hebrews 7:21). This oath, quoted from Psalm 110:4, is "The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent." This oath guarantees that Jesus remains a priest forever and makes his priesthood superior and unchangeable.
G3728.portee: The divine oath addressed to Jesus reveals the solidity and eternity of the salvation we have in him. Unlike a mere human promise, God's oath is an absolute guarantee that cannot fail — it is a foundation of trust for the believer who relies on Christ's perpetual intercession before the Father.

sens: To leap forward with great speed, in an impetuous and sudden manner
To act with urgency, without thinking, under the effect of an impulse
To throw oneself together towards the same place or action
G3729.detail:
1. To rush describes a violent and rapid movement: the herd of pigs rushes down the steep bank into the sea (Matthew 8:32, Mark 5:13, Luke 8:33), driven by a force it cannot restrain. It is the image of a mass that irresistibly rushes towards its fall.
2. The word also characterizes action under the influence of an impulse: the people of the synagogue rush at Stephen to stone him (Acts 7:57), without waiting, driven by anger. The speed testifies to the intensity of the feeling that carries them away.
3. Finally, to rush can describe a collective and sudden action: the entire crowd rushes to the theater to see Paul (Acts 19:29), driven by the confusion and excitement of the moment.
G3729.origine: The word comes from the Greek root hormḗ, which literally means impulse, momentum, assault. It is a movement of the soul that pushes to act without delay. The root refers to the image of an army's attack or a horse's gallop — something that charges forward without restraint. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb often translates the Hebrew word meaning to turn or to throw oneself towards.
G3729.emploi: The verb hormaō appears five times in the New Testament, always in the Gospels and in Acts. Three times, it describes the herd of pigs rushing into the sea after the expulsion of demons (Matthew, Mark, Luke): it is the same event recounted by three witnesses. Twice, it describes a sudden collective action: the listeners of Stephen rush at him in Acts 7:57, and the crowd of Ephesus rushes to the theater in Acts 19:29. In each case, the verb emphasizes the absence of deliberation, the urgency, and the intensity of the movement.
G3729.portee: This word helps us recognize how the powers of evil lose all control before the power of Jesus: the demons flee, and the pigs they have seized rush towards death. It also shows how a crowd can be quickly swept away by collective emotion, sometimes into violence (against Stephen), sometimes into confusion (in Ephesus). It is a lesson on the fragility of our discernment when we act under the influence of impulse.

sens: violent or impetuous movement
hostile movement, assault
concerted action, common agreement
G3730.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a violent and irresistible movement. In James 3:4, large ships are driven by impetuous winds with such an impulse that they must be steered by a rudder. It is the image of a force that carries everything away in its path.
2. The impulse can also take on an aggressive character, a movement of assault or revolt. In Acts 14:5, the pagan crowd and the Jews move together to attack Paul and Barnabas: it is the impulse of hostility, the clan that rises and rushes forward.
3. By extension, the word expresses an action carried out together, an agreement that drives people to act in concert. The pagans and the Jews do not act separately: there is a shared impulse, a common impetus that unites them in the same movement.
G3730.origine: The Greek word hormē comes from a root that evokes bursting forth and impulse. It literally designates what pushes, what makes move — the equivalent of the movement of an animal rushing at its prey. In Hebrew, this impetuous movement is often rendered by words related to rushing or assault.
G3730.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament. In James 3:4, it describes the impulse of the winds that drive the ships, a natural and physical phenomenon. In Acts 14:5, it describes a social and hostile impulse: the crowd moves as one clan to attack the apostles. The basic meaning — violent and impetuous movement — thus nuances between the physical (the wind on the sea) and the collective psychology (the angry crowd).
G3730.portee: This word reminds the reader of the power of forces that carry us away: the passions of the crowd, the hostility of the world, or simply the impetuosity of the wind and waves. Just as a ship needs a rudder to master the impulse of the winds, the believer needs wisdom and the Spirit to control the impulses of his heart and flesh.

sens: Brutal impulse, violent and impetuous movement
Sudden and irresistible force that overturns or destroys
G3731.detail: 1. The word first evokes an impulse, a movement that starts with force and impetuosity, like a wave crashing or an object thrown with power. In Revelation 18:21, the angel throws a millstone into the sea "with violence": it is this brutal impulse, this blow struck with force, that precipitates Babylon into its ruin. 2. More broadly, it is the irresistible force of an event that falls and destroys. The violence in question here is not cruel or wicked, but the overwhelming effect of an action — Babylon will be engulfed not by a person striking it, but by the force of divine judgment executed with suddenness and inexorable power.
G3731.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb *hormáō*, which means "to rush, to leap forward." It is the movement of one who charges ahead, like a horse that gets carried away. The Greek Old Testament uses it to translate the Hebrew *'ebrah* (fury, anger): the basic meaning is therefore this unleashed force, this energy that suddenly breaks free. The nominal form *hormēma* fixes this image of the blow, the shock, the violent movement as such.
G3731.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 18:21, in the vision of the judgment of Babylon. The mighty angel throws the millstone "with violence" (*hormēma*), to show that the fall of the great city will not be slow or gradual, but sudden, irresistible, overwhelming. This apocalyptic context enriches the meaning: it is not a human violence or malice, but the execution of divine judgment that falls with inevitable force. The word emphasizes the inescapable and striking nature of the punishment.
G3731.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that God's judgment, when executed, does not drag on: it comes with a decisive force that annihilates what opposes his will. This invites us to take the Lord's warnings seriously and to recognize that his justice is not passive, but active and fearsome. It is an invitation to place oneself on the right side of divine judgment.

sens: Winged creature capable of flying, vertebrate animal with feathers
Figuratively, an unclean creature or symbol of desolation in apocalyptic visions
G3732.detail:
1. The word simply refers to a bird, a living creature with wings and feathers. It is the ordinary animal that everyone knows. In Revelation 19:17, birds fly in the sky and gather at the call of an angel, demonstrating their natural mobility.
2. In the prophetic visions of Revelation, birds take on symbolic value. In Revelation 18:2, unclean birds settle in the ruins of Babylon, evoking desolation and divine judgment. In Revelation 19:21, birds feed on the corpses of God's enemies, a stark image of final punishment. Here, the bird becomes the visible sign of ruin and destruction.
G3732.origine: The Greek word *orneon* is the neuter form of *ornéos* ("of a bird"), derived from the noun *ornis* (bird). It is a simple and ancient word in Greek, attested as early as Homer. In the Greek Old Testament, *orneon* generally translates the Hebrew *tzippor*, the common word for bird. This root simply expresses the natural reality of the winged creature.
G3732.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in Revelation (18:2; 19:17, 21). It is a relatively rare term. John uses it exclusively in contexts of prophetic vision, where birds play a dramatic role: either as inhabitants of the ruins of Babylon or as executors of final judgment. The word remains concrete — these are real birds — but acquires a symbolic charge: they embody the visible consequence of God's judgment on injustice.
G3732.portee: For the reader of Revelation, the bird is the living witness of God's justice. When the birds gather over the remnants of evil, it makes divine judgment visible and irrevocable. It is an invitation to meditate on the final punishment of injustice, but also to recognize that God governs all creation to fulfill His purpose. The bird reminds us that nothing in the universe escapes the control and judgment of the Lord.

sens: Female domestic bird of the farm, which lays eggs and hatches its young
Biblical image of maternal protection and gathering
G3733.detail:
1. The word simply refers to a hen, the female bird that households raised on the farm for its eggs and meat. It is a humble, ordinary animal, well known to all peasants and townspeople of Palestine.
2. In the mouth of Jesus, the hen becomes a touching image of maternal tenderness. When Jesus says to Jerusalem, "how often I have longed to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings" (Matthew 23:37 and Luke 13:34), He uses this familiar and maternal gesture — the hen protecting her brood — to express His patient love and desire to save the people, despite their refusal. The hen here represents divine care, simple yet profound.
G3733.origine: The Greek word ornis comes from an ancient root that expresses the cry of the bird. In Hebrew, the Old Testament mostly uses different terms for birds; the Greek of the Septuagint sought the word that best corresponded to these realities. Ornis is the common word in classical Greek for any bird, and then more specifically the domestic hen in the context of the New Testament.
G3733.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both times by Jesus, in an identical passage reported by Matthew and Luke: the lament over Jerusalem. Jesus, out of love for the city and its children, wanted to gather them "as a hen gathers her chicks" or "her brood." This is therefore not a zoological description of the bird, but a metaphor of protection and maternal love: Jesus places Himself at the heart of the people as a protective mother, and this image of the maternal hen reinforces the intensity of His rejection by Jerusalem.
G3733.portee: This simple and concrete word shows us how Jesus used everyday images to speak of His love. The hen that protects her brood under her wings becomes a window into the heart of Jesus: His tenderness, His patience, His desire to gather and save despite indifference or hostility. For the believer, this word invites meditation on the maternal love of Jesus and on our responsibility to respond to this call for protection and unity.

sens: Limit, border marking the territory of a region or a people
Set of limits that delineate a space, a domain
G3734.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a physical limit drawn or fixed to mark where one territory ends and another begins. In Acts 17:26, Paul speaks of the "boundaries" of the dwelling of nations: God has established for each people the geographical borders, the limits of the land they inhabit.
2. In the plural, the word expands to signify the entirety of delimitations, the contours of an assigned region. It can also evoke the limits placed on a domain or authority: it is a biblical thought that God sets the limits of each thing according to His wisdom.
G3734.origine: The Greek word comes from two elements: "horos" (boundary, limit, border) and "tithenai" (to place, establish, fix). It literally means "the action of fixing boundaries." The root "horos" appears in many ancient Greek compounds related to the delimitation of space. This term translates the Hebrew idea of "geboul" (boundary, limit of territory).
G3734.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 17:26. Paul uses it in his speech at the Areopagus in Athens to affirm that it is God who has determined the boundaries of the territory inhabited by each nation. This choice of vocabulary emphasizes divine sovereignty over the political geography of the world: no boundary is established by chance, but everything has been ordered by the creator. The use of the plural ("boundaries") highlights the multiplicity of peoples and the diversity of assigned territories.
G3734.portee: This verse reminds Christians that God exercises total sovereignty over nations, peoples, and their territories. No human power can permanently alter what God has established. It is a call to recognize that behind geopolitical events lies divine order, and to place trust in the one who governs nations rather than in human forces.

sens: Natural elevated relief, rocky mass that rises above the plain
Mountain range or mountainous region, particularly the heights of the land
Place of retreat, isolation, or solitude
Difficult obstacle to overcome, great difficulty
Seat of divine manifestations, place of encounter with God
G3735.detail: 1. The mountain is primarily a physical relief, a peak or a well-defined geographical height: Jesus sees "all the kingdoms of the world" from a "very high mountain" (Matthew 4:8), or goes up the mountain to be transfigured (Mark 9:2). 2. The word also refers to an entire mountainous region, especially the heights above the Sea of Galilee where Jesus often retreats: there he calls his twelve apostles (Mark 3:13) and delivers the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:1). 3. The mountain evokes isolation and solitude: Jesus goes alone "to a solitary high mountain" to pray (Matthew 14:23), or withdraws into the mountains when the crowd seeks him (Luke 6:12). 4. Symbolically, moving a mountain means overcoming an almost impossible difficulty: "If you had faith... you would say to this mountain: Move..." (Matthew 17:20, 1 Corinthians 13:2). 5. The mountain is the setting for encounters with God: Moses receives the Decalogue on Mount Sinai (Acts 7:30), Jesus is transfigured before three apostles (Mark 9:2), and Revelation speaks of the heavenly "Mount Zion" (Revelation 14:1).
G3735.origine: The Greek word oros comes from an Indo-European root meaning "elevation." It translates the Hebrew har in the Greek Old Testament, which refers to both geographical reliefs and important places in the history of salvation. Mountains play a major theological role in the Bible: they are natural boundaries, refuges, and especially places where God manifests Himself (Sinai, Horeb, Zion). The word has retained this dual meaning: geographical and spiritual.
G3735.emploi: The word oros appears 65 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew and Mark. It first refers to real and named mountains: the Mount of Olives near Jerusalem (Matthew 21:1, Luke 19:29), Mount Sinai (Acts 7:30), the heavenly Mount Zion (Revelation 14:1). In the Gospels, the mountain is the favorite setting for Jesus' actions: a place of transfiguration (Mark 9:2), solitary prayer (Luke 6:12), the Sermon (Matthew 5:1). It also signifies an entire region: "the mountain" (singular) refers to the heights above the Sea of Galilee, a space for retreat. Finally, in a proverbial usage inherited from Judaism, "moving a mountain" becomes the image of a human impossibility overcome by faith (Matthew 17:20, Mark 11:23).
G3735.portee: For the believing reader, the mountain reminds us that God manifests and acts in real space, at concrete locations. It invites us to seek solitude to pray like Jesus (Luke 6:12), and to understand that nothing is impossible for those who have faith (Matthew 17:20). It also symbolizes the obstacles of the Christian life: what seems insurmountable in our eyes must be entrusted to God. Finally, it spiritually situates the believer: the heavenly mountain of Zion (Hebrews 12:22) is the true goal of faith.

sens: Make a hole in the ground by moving it
Dig a well, a pit, or a winepress
G3736.detail: 1. The verb describes the concrete action of digging: removing earth to form a hollow. In the parable of the householder (Matthew 21:33), a winepress is "dug" — that is, a vat carved from rock or deeply excavated — to tread the grapes and extract the juice. The image is one of patient and determined work: an implement is driven into the ground to create a void. 2. The word is also used to simply dig the earth to hide something. In Matthew 25:18, the one who received a talent digs a hole in the ground to bury his master's money — a furtive action that reveals his fear and inaction. Thus, digging is both a technical act and a human gesture laden with meaning: one digs out of necessity (a winepress for the harvest), or out of fear (to hide).
G3736.origine: The verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of making a hole, of digging. In the Hebrew of the Greek Old Testament, it often translates חָפַר (haphar: to dig, to excavate) and כָּרָה (karah: to dig, to mine), very concrete verbs describing the work of men who shape the soil.
G3736.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Gospel. It appears in two parallel versions of the same parable (Matthew 21:33 and Mark 12:1): the householder "digs" a winepress, showing the care he takes of his vineyard before entrusting it to the vinedressers. A third occurrence (Matthew 25:18) shows it in a completely different light: the lazy servant digs the earth not to create something, but to steal — a sterile and hidden act. The context changes the moral weight of the verb: digging can be a sign of investment and work, or conversely, of disguised inaction.
G3736.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on what he builds or hides. In the parable of the householder, digging the winepress shows a thoughtful and responsible work: investing for the harvest. In the case of the lazy servant, digging reveals the sterility of fear: instead of making his talent grow, he hides it. The believer is called to dig where it is right — to prepare, to sow, to build — and not to settle for hiding.

sens: Child deprived of his father or both parents
Abandoned person, without support, isolated
G3737.detail:
1. The literal meaning refers to a child who has lost his father or parents. This is a situation of vulnerability and material deprivation well known in Israel, hence the importance that the Law places on the protection of orphans. James 1:27 shows this: visiting orphans is an act of faith and concrete charity.
2. The word also takes on a broader meaning: one who feels abandoned, without a protector, left to himself. Jesus uses it in John 14:18 to reassure his disciples: although deprived of his physical presence after his departure, they will not be "orphans," left without a comforter or guide.
G3737.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that evokes absence and deprivation. It translates the Hebrew "yatôm," which designates a minor without a father. The family of this word in Greek always describes a condition of lack or loss: orphan, but also widow, devoid of resources.
G3737.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament. In James 1:27, it is part of a strong Old Testament tradition: protecting orphans is a work of mercy that God values. In John 14:18, Jesus changes its usage: he uses it not of simple fatherless children, but of his disciples, to express their spiritual distress after his ascension to heaven, and to announce to them that they will not remain in this state of abandonment.
G3737.portee: This word reminds us that the Gospel also cares for the most vulnerable. For the believer, it evokes two truths: first, concrete faith is manifested in relieving orphans and widows; second, even when we feel abandoned or alone, Christ assures us that he does not leave us as orphans, but sends us the Holy Spirit to comfort and guide us.

sens: Movement of the body in time with music
Joyful or festive reaction to an invitation
Figure of speech for an absence of appropriate emotional response
G3738.detail:
1. To dance is to perform movements of the body in rhythm with music — it is the concrete physical action. When the daughter of Herodias "danced" at Herod's feast (Matthew 14:6), she was providing a danced entertainment before the king's court.

2. In the context of a feast or celebration, dance expresses joy and joyful acceptance of an invitation to rejoice together. This is what Jesus indirectly reproaches his contemporaries for: they received an invitation to joy (the joyful music) but did not respond with the dance that would be appropriate (Matthew 11:17).

3. As a figure of speech, not dancing when the flute is played means refusing to respond appropriately to a call to joy or emotion — it is ignoring what should evoke a heartfelt reaction. Jesus uses it to describe unbelief: people reject both the joy he brings and the repentance he asks for (Luke 7:32).
G3738.origine: The Greek verb comes from a root that denotes ordered movement, the rhythm of the body. The Hebrew רָקַד (raqad) that it often translates in the Greek Old Testament has the same concrete meaning: to dance, to leap for joy. Dance in antiquity was a natural social and religious gesture, linked to celebration, festivity, and collective emotional expression.
G3738.emploi: The verb appears only four times in the New Testament, always in the Synoptic Gospels. It is first used to describe the concrete action of the daughter of Herodias dancing at the king's court (Matthew 14:6 and Mark 6:22) — it is a festive entertainment that impresses Herod. It then appears twice in the words of Jesus in parables: he uses it to criticize the refusal to respond joyfully to the preaching (Matthew 11:17 and Luke 7:32). In these last two cases, not dancing symbolizes a heart closed to God's invitation.
G3738.portee: This word reminds us that joy and celebration are natural and expected responses to God's grace. Jesus reproaches his adversaries for refusing this joy, for remaining closed to what should delight their hearts.
