For the believer, it is an invitation not to be paralyzed by unbelief or mistrust, but to welcome the good news with joy.

sens: relative pronoun designating a person or thing in relation to a preceding noun or noun group
demonstrative pronoun (this one, that one) to indicate a particular character or object, often in the nominative
the neuter to designate a thing, action, fact, word, or entire concept
linking word that introduces a relationship of cause, purpose, or consequence
interrogative or indefinite pronoun with the particles ἄν or καί
G3739.detail:
1. It is a relative pronoun: it connects a person or thing to a name mentioned just before. For example, in Matthew 1:16, "Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus": the word "whom" refers to Mary and introduces new information about her. In John 11:46, "what Jesus had done": the pronoun "what" connects the action to Jesus.

2. It can function as a demonstrative pronoun (this one, that one), pointing to a character or situation without an explicit antecedent. In Mark 15:23, "ὅς δέ" (literally "but he") presents a character in isolation.

3. In the neuter form (ὅ, "this"), it designates an abstract thing, fact, word, or concept rather than a person. For example, in Acts 21:24, "what they have heard about you": the neuter encompasses an entire rumor or matter. In Hebrews 4:13, "to whom we must give account" uses the relative to connect the accountability to God.

4. With certain prepositions (ἀνθ᾽ ὧν = "because of which", ἐξ οὗ = "since"), it expresses a cause, reason, or consequence. In Luke 1:20, ἀνθ᾽ ὧν introduces the reason for a sanction.

5. With the particles ἄν, ἐάν, or καί, it takes a conditional, indefinite, or appositional value, as in Mark 3:19 or Romans 5:2.
G3739.origine: This word comes from ancient Greek and remains one of the most common pronouns. It originates from a common Indo-European root shared by interrogative and relative pronouns. In the Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament), it often translates the Hebrew אֲשֶׁר (asher), the quintessential Hebrew relative pronoun. This kinship shows that both languages, Hebrew and Greek, used a similar type of word to link propositions and speak of already named persons or things.
G3739.emploi: This word is one of the most frequent in the New Testament, with over 1,200 occurrences. It serves three main roles: relative pronoun (which relates information to a person or thing), demonstrative pronoun (which points to a character or situation), and linking pronoun in causal or final structures. In the Gospels, it connects Jesus' teaching or actions to people or principles: for example, "he who wishes to follow me" in Matthew 10:38 or "what he says" in Luke 6:46. In the Epistles, it structures theological arguments by linking truths (for example, in Romans 2:29). Its case (nominative, genitive, dative, accusative) changes according to its grammatical function, but its meaning remains: to connect, identify, clarify.
G3739.portee: This small word allows linking God's promises and biblical teachings to the concrete life of the reader. When Jesus says "he who wishes to follow me" (ὃς), he addresses his word to each one: the relative makes the reader a participant. Similarly, when Paul speaks of "what he received from the Lord", the neuter "what" encompasses a spiritual reality that touches the entire community. This pronoun also helps to chain cause and consequence: understanding why something happens (through the causal structures it introduces) illuminates God's wisdom and justice.

sens: on each occasion when, each time something occurs
G3740.detail: 1. The word expresses repetition: each occasion when an action recurs, it happens again. It is equivalent to "each time that" or "whenever". In 1 Corinthians 11:25-26, Jesus institutes the Lord's Supper by saying that the disciples must celebrate it "whenever" they drink it — meaning that each celebration of the Lord's Supper renews this memorial. In Revelation 11:6, it describes how the two witnesses have the power to strike the earth "whenever" they wish — at each act of their will, the power is exercised.
G3740.origine: The word comes from ὅσος ("as much as, as great as, so much") with the suffix -ακις which marks repetition. It is a relative adverb of frequency: it links two actions by showing that one accompanies the other each time it occurs.
G3740.emploi: The word appears only 3 times in Greek in the New Testament and is always used to express iteration — the fact that something repeats on each new occasion. In 1 Corinthians 11:25-26, it frames the institution of the Lord's Supper: each future celebration reactivates the memorial of Christ's death. In Revelation 11:6, it punctuates the description of the power of the two witnesses, showing that each time they decide, their power is exercised. It is a technical word in discourse that links a condition or occasion to its repeated effect.
G3740.portee: This word invites the reader to understand that certain acts do not occur just once, but regularly return with the same meaning. For the Lord's Supper, it reminds us that each celebration is not a new invention but a faithful reprise of the act instituted by Jesus. This underscores the importance of continuity in the Christian life: obeying once is not enough; it is the faithful repetition that manifests our commitment.

sens: belonging to God and worship, set apart from the profane
free from guilt and moral defilement
conforming to justice and righteousness
(when speaking of God) just and worthy of reverence
G3741.detail: 1. The word primarily designates what is reserved for God, consecrated to worship: the "holy graces promised to David" (Acts 13:34) are the blessings that God has given according to His covenant. 2. It also characterizes moral purity and the absence of guilt: the "pure hands" (1 Timothy 2:8) express a prayer without ulterior motives, without anger, with a clear spirit and heart. 3. Holiness also signifies justice and righteousness: a bishop must be "holy" (Titus 1:8) in the sense of virtuous and blameless. Jesus is described as "holy, innocent, unstained" (Hebrews 7:26), meaning perfectly just and separated from sin. 4. When applied to God, the word expresses His just and supreme nature, worthy of praise: "Who would not fear the Lord and glorify Your name? For You alone are holy" (Revelation 15:4).
G3741.origine: The word comes from a root expressing the idea of separation, of what is set apart. In ancient Hebrew, it primarily translates 'hasîd ("pious, faithful"), which refers to loyalty to God's covenant. Biblical holiness is therefore not merely ritual purity, but a rectitude of heart: to be holy is to be separated from sin and in accordance with God's justice.
G3741.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the New Testament, concentrated in the Pastoral Epistles and the book of Revelation. It first describes virtuous and reliable men (Titus 1:8), then Jesus Christ, who embodies perfect holiness (Hebrews 7:26; Acts 2:27, 13:35, where the Psalms refer to Him as the "Holy One"). In the final doxologies, God Himself is praised as the only holy one (Revelation 15:4, 16:5). Holiness thus characterizes those who are faithful to the covenant and, most importantly, God and His Messiah.
G3741.portee: This word reminds the believer that holiness is not about external purification or asceticism, but about a conformity of the heart to divine justice. By calling Jesus "holy," Scripture affirms that He alone is free from guilt and able to reconcile humanity with God. For the Christian, it is an invitation to purify one's heart and actions, to pray with right intentions, and to recognize that only God possesses absolute holiness.

sens: State of one who is pure, separated from evil and consecrated to God
Pious and just conduct towards God and towards men
Moral quality produced by truth and created in us by God
G3742.detail:
1. Holiness is primarily a separation from evil and a consecration to God: it is the state of one who belongs to God and lives in harmony with His will. In Luke 1:75, the angel speaks of walking "in holiness and righteousness all the days of our life," which shows that holiness is a concrete way of living, day by day, separated from sin.
2. Holiness manifests itself in pious conduct towards God and others: it includes justice (doing what is right) and expresses our respect for God. It is a life that pleases God and reflects Him.
3. In Ephesians 4:24, Paul speaks of "putting on the new man, created according to God in righteousness and holiness produced by truth": this shows that holiness is not something we create ourselves, but a work of God in us, engendered by divine truth.
G3742.origine: The word comes from the adjective ὅσιος (hosios), which means "pious, holy, consecrated to God." In the Greek Old Testament, it translates Hebrew terms such as יֹשֶׁר (yosher, righteousness) and תֹּם or תָּמִים (tom/tamim, integrity, perfection). The Greek word emphasizes piety towards God — a right relationship with Him — rather than merely ritual purity. It is a lived, moral, and spiritual holiness.
G3742.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, making it a particularly significant term when it arises. In Luke 1:75, in the canticle of Zechariah, holiness is an ideal that the redeemed people must live: to walk before God in holiness. In Ephesians 4:24, Paul always links it to righteousness, emphasizing that it is "created according to God" — it comes from God Himself, not from our efforts. These two uses show that holiness is both a call to moral conduct and a gift from the Lord.
G3742.portee: For the Christian, this word reveals that holiness is not an unattainable perfection, but a concrete life of separation from evil and consecration to God, day by day. It is also an encouragement: holiness is not something we must create by our strength, but a work that God produces in us through His truth. It calls for both our moral commitment and our trust in God's transformative action.

sens: Pious way of living and submission to God
Behavior in accordance with divine holiness
Moral attitude respectful of law and justice
G3743.detail:
1. This word describes a way of living that reflects piety towards God: it is to conduct oneself with respect and reverential fear, in recognition of who God is. In 1 Thessalonians 2:10, Paul speaks of his "holy conduct" before the believers, showing how he lived a life of religious devotion and honor towards God.
2. It is a morally elevated behavior, characterized by holiness and purity. Paul associates this conduct with justice ("just") and blamelessness, together forming a portrait of an irreproachable life.
3. The word emphasizes the aspect of respect for law and moral rectitude: living in a way that honors God and does not hurt anyone's conscience. It is an integrity that touches both the relationship with God and with others.
G3743.origine: This word comes from the Greek adjective "hosios" (holy, pious), which expresses holiness in the sense of what pleases God and aligns with His nature. The root evokes the idea of religious respect and separation from evil. In ancient Hebrew, this meaning is close to words expressing holiness and piety: the common idea is that of a consecrated and pure life, pleasing to the divine.
G3743.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Thessalonians 2:10. Paul uses it to defend his ministry and that of his companions before the Thessalonians, testifying to the moral quality of their life among them. It is not a common word, but a solemn and strong term, chosen to express the gravity of spiritual commitment. Paul combines it with "justly" and "blamelessly" to form a triple portrait of complete virtue.
G3743.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Christian faith is not limited to beliefs: it must manifest itself in a concrete life of holiness and justice. For the Christian, it is a call to allow God to transform one's daily behavior, so that one's conduct reflects the respect and love one has for God. It is also an invitation to seek forgiveness when one strays from this, for only Christ makes this true holiness possible.

sens: Olfactory sensation released by a substance
G3744.detail: 1. The odor is what we smell with our nose: a physical sensation produced by a substance. When Mary pours nard perfume on Jesus' feet, "the house was filled with the odor of the perfume" (John 12:3) — it is the concrete odor that spreads throughout the room. 2. By extension, the odor becomes the image of an invisible influence that spreads. Paul writes that God "spreads through us in every place the odor of His knowledge" (2 Corinthians 2:14): we do not see this odor, but it spreads everywhere and touches people. 3. Finally, the odor represents the spiritual effect of our life or sacrifice before God. Christ's offering is "a fragrant odor" accepted by God (Ephesians 5:2; Philippians 4:18), like the ancient worship where sacrifices were offered whose smoke ascended to God. The odor signals that the sacrifice is received and pleasing.
G3744.origine: The Greek word osmē comes from a root that evokes the sensation of smell. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew word "reïah" (odor, scent). This image of odor spreading invisibly has naturally served to express how spiritual influence, knowledge, or divine favor extends and touches people — invisible like the odor, but real and perceptible in its effects.
G3744.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament, always in Paul and in the Gospels. It first denotes physical odor: the perfume that fills the house of Simon the Pharisee (John 12:3). But Paul mainly uses it in a spiritual or sacrificial sense. In 2 Corinthians 2:14-16, the odor represents how the knowledge of Christ spreads through us — but it does not have the same effect on everyone: it is "the odor of death" for those who resist, "the odor of life" for those who believe. This dual image emphasizes that our Christian life is never spiritually neutral. In Ephesians 5:2 and Philippians 4:18, the odor evokes the acceptable sacrifice to God — it takes up the image from the Old Testament where sacrifices were offered "of sweet odor" (in Hebrew: "reïah nihoah"). Thus, the life of the Christian offered to God and the love of giving are presented as a sacrifice that pleases God.
G3744.portee: This word teaches the Christian that their life is not without spiritual effect: it emits an "odor" that spreads around them, for good or for ill — it speaks of Christ or against Him. It also invites one to offer their life to God not as an obligation, but as a precious perfume, a free offering that God receives with pleasure. This image makes concrete the gift of self: it is not a calculation, it is a generosity that "smells good" in heaven.

sens: the totality, the whole without exception
the entire quantity or number of something
each thing, each person taken individually
to the extent that, as much as
as long as
in comparison, all the more that
G3745.detail:
1. The primary and most common meaning: the totality of something, leaving nothing aside. In Matthew 7:12, "all that you wish men to do for you" means each of the things, without exception, that you desire to receive. In Mark 3:10, "all who had diseases" refers to the totality of the sick present, each one of them.
2. The complete quantity or number: "all that he needs" (Luke 11:8) means the entirety of his needs, the whole sum. This conveys the idea of numerical or quantitative completeness.
3. Each individual element considered in its entirety: "all who have sinned" (Romans 2:12) refers to each sinner, but viewed as a complete class. The word encompasses both unity and multiplicity.
4. In a comparison, "as much as" or "to the extent that": Hebrews 3:3 uses this sense to establish a proportional relationship.
5. "As long as" or "while": Matthew 9:15, "while the bridegroom is with them," where the word marks duration and temporal extent.
6. In comparison of intensity: "all the more" or "as much as," to express a relationship of degree or relative magnitude.
G3745.origine: This word comes from the Greek root that expresses the idea of "how much" or "to what extent." It is correlative to the word τοσοῦτος ("as much," "so great"), just as the French "tout" corresponds to "tant." In Hebrew from the Old Testament, it often translates the word כָּל ("kol"), which has exactly the same meaning of totality. The Greek family also includes the adverb ὅπως ("how") and the interrogative τίς ("who? what?"). The starting image is that of "measuring" or "counting": the word encompasses a notion of quantification and completeness.
G3745.emploi: This word is among the most frequent in the New Testament, used about 100 times. It appears in all the Gospels, then in Acts, the Pauline epistles, and Revelation. Its use varies according to grammatical context: in the nominative, it can be a subject ("all who...") but most often functions as an adjective or object pronoun ("all that..."). With the subjunctive or with the particle ἄν, it takes on a conditional or indefinite nuance ("as long as," "whatever"). In comparisons, it associates with other particles (ἐφ᾽ ὅσον, καθ᾽ ὅσον) to express a proportion or causal relationship. Its main translations in French (Segond) are "all," "this," "all," "that," which shows the flexibility of this word that adapts to various syntactic structures.
G3745.portee: This word emphasizes the integrity and completeness of God's action or promise. When Jesus says "all that you ask in prayer" (Matthew 21:22), He unreservedly affirms the scope of the divine promise. Likewise, "all who" believe receive the right to become children of God (John 1:12), highlighting the universality of the Gospel. For the believer, this word invites total trust in the word of Christ and unconditional obedience to His will.

sens: Bony structure of the skeleton
Remains of the dead, bones
Material substance of the living body
G3747.detail:
1. The bone is the hard element that forms the skeleton of the human and animal body. It is the solid material that gives structure to the body — it could not stand without its bones. The Bible speaks of the broken bones of Christ on the cross (John 19:36), thus respecting what had been prophesied.

2. The word also refers to the remains of a dead person, the bones left after decomposition. The tombs of the Pharisees are described as full of the bones of the dead (Matthew 23:27), an image of a power that is only outward: beautiful on the outside, impure on the inside.

3. By extension, the bone represents the very substance of the living body, what constitutes it physically. When the resurrected Christ shows His bones to His disciples (Luke 24:39), He proves that His body is real, not a mere ghost: He has flesh and bones, tangible proof of His resurrection.
G3747.origine: The Greek word ὀστέον comes from an ancient Indo-European root that designates the bony structure. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament primarily translates the term עֶצֶם (etsem) with this word, which carries the same meaning. The form can contract to ὀστοῦν in Attic Greek. The family of the word in Greek includes terms related to the structure and solidity of the body.
G3747.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and in the epistle to the Hebrews. Matthew uses it to speak of the bones in the whitened tombs, a symbol of religious hypocrisy. Luke employs it when the resurrected Christ allows Himself to be touched to prove His bodily reality. John cites a messianic prophecy: no bone of the Messiah will be broken. Hebrews uses it figuratively when Joseph, by faith, gives orders concerning his bones — an act of trust in God's promise. The word thus serves to express the tangible reality of the body or, conversely, the vanity of what is merely appearance.
G3747.portee: For the believer, the word reminds two essential truths. First, the bodily reality is important: the resurrection of Jesus is not a spiritual illusion, but a resurrection of flesh and bones. Secondly, the bones become an image of faith: entrusting one's bones to God, like Joseph, means trusting Him even in what we leave behind. It is a lesson of hope beyond death.

sens: Indeterminate person in a general statement (‘the one who’, ‘whoever’)
Specific person or thing defined by a particular quality (‘the one who is such’)
In a proposition introducing a cause or consequence (‘since’, ‘given that’)
Close to the simple relative ‘who’ without nuance of generality
G3748.detail:
1. This word designates any person, indefinite, in statements that apply to all. For example: ‘Whoever looks at a woman to lust for her’ (Matthew 5:28, implicit in usages) means any man in that situation. ‘Whoever wants to come after me, let him deny himself’ (Luke 14:27) addresses anyone, without exception.
2. Sometimes, this word remains linked to a specific person or thing, but it is designated by its nature or quality, rather than by its name: ‘a ruler who will shepherd Israel’ (Matthew 2:6) speaks of the Messiah by describing his function. Similarly: ‘women who had followed Jesus’ (Matthew 27:55) indicates specific women we know, but characterized by what they did.
3. Occasionally, the relative clause expresses the reason or the result of an action. For example: ‘This has distressed me; for I am alone and desolate’ where the second part explains the first. This word then introduces a nuance of causality or consequence.
4. In later texts and in the last layer of the New Testament, this word closely resembles the simple ‘who’ without significant difference. It is a natural evolution of Greek: the two forms eventually become indistinguishable.
G3748.origine: This word is formed from ὅς (‘who’) and τις (‘a certain one’, ‘someone’). The union of the two produces the idea of ‘the one who, whoever he may be’ — a generalization. In Latin, this would correspond to ‘quisquis’ (who + who), which also doubles the pronoun. The root goes back to the Indo-Europeans. In Hebrew, the Old Testament often uses similar constructions, such as the repetition of the pronoun or the addition of words to express a generality.
G3748.emploi: The word appears 139 times in the New Testament, almost always in the nominative (subject case). It is extremely frequent in Matthew, Luke, and in Acts, especially in the words of Jesus and in the narratives of the apostles. Matthew uses it for parables and general teachings (‘the tax collector who prays’, Luke 18:13 implicit). In Acts, it describes specific circumstances (‘those who received the word’, Acts 2:41 implicit). As time goes on, in Revelation and in later epistles, its distinction from the simple ‘who’ fades: the two become interchangeable.
G3748.portee: This word teaches the reader that the Bible often speaks in universal principles: a word or a judgment addresses whoever finds themselves in that situation, without exception. This makes every promise and every command personal. The Christian understands that the Gospel is not just about a closed group, but ‘whoever believes’—a universal and radically inclusive invitation.

sens: Made with clay, in pottery
Fragile, ordinary, of little value
Humble, intended for common or base use
G3749.detail:
1. The word literally designates an object shaped from clay, such as everyday vases or pottery. In 2 Corinthians 4:7, Paul speaks of ‘clay jars’ in which Christians carry the treasure of the Gospel: it is a concrete image of inexpensive and fragile ceramic containers that were commonly used.
2. These clay jars are by nature fragile and easily breakable, unlike gold or silver vessels that last. This fragility becomes an image: it symbolizes human weakness. Paul uses it to show that it is precisely because we are weak that the power comes from God, not from us.
3. In 2 Timothy 2:20, clay jars are contrasted with gold and silver vessels of a great house: some are ‘vessels of honor’, others ‘for base use’. Here, the adjective emphasizes the social and moral contrast between what is noble and what is humble, ordinary, or despised.
G3749.origine: The Greek word comes from the root ‘ostrakon’ (ὄστρακον), which means a shard of pottery, a tile, or a clay vessel. In ancient Hebrew, it is the word חֶרֶשׂ (herés) that designates fragile pottery. The image is that of the potter's work: clay is shaped to make useful but ephemeral containers. The root evokes the idea of a friable substance, molded and fired.
G3749.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Greek of the New Testament, both times by Paul. In 2 Corinthians 4:7, it serves a profound theological image: the apostles are ‘clay jars’ containing a divine treasure, which magnifies the power of God by highlighting the fragility of his instruments. In 2 Timothy 2:20, Paul uses it more generally to classify the utensils of a house according to their function and status: some for honor, others for base use. In both cases, the fragility and humility of the material carry a spiritual teaching.
G3749.portee: This word reminds the Christian that he is weak and fragile, but that it is precisely his condition that highlights the power and glory of God. Far from being a humiliation, this fragility becomes a grace: it prevents pride and directs all gaze toward Him who alone is strong. It is a call to humility and trust in divine sufficiency.

sens: the sensory ability to perceive odors
the sense of the human body located in the nose
G3750.detail: 1. The sense of smell is the sense that allows the human body to perceive and recognize odors — such as when one smells a flower or the aroma of a dish. It is a biological and sensory capacity among others (sight, hearing, touch). In 1 Corinthians 12:17, Paul uses the sense of smell to illustrate how the human body cannot consist of just one part: it needs several different senses, just as the Church needs various gifts.
G3750.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb ‘osphraínomai’ which literally means ‘to smell, to sniff’, and evokes the natural and immediate action of perceiving an odor. This term expresses a very concrete sensory faculty, well rooted in bodily experience. The word is used only once in the New Testament.
G3750.emploi: The word ‘sense of smell’ appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Corinthians 12:17. The Apostle Paul speaks of the sense of smell as one of the senses of the human body, alongside sight and hearing. He uses it as an example in his reflection on the diversity of gifts within the Church: just as the human body needs several distinct senses to function, the Christian Church needs various different gifts to be complete and alive.
G3750.portee: This word reminds the believer that the human body — and by extension the Church — is a reality composed of several complementary parts. No part is superfluous, and each has its own function. This invites the Christian to value the diversity of gifts and not to seek to do everything in the same way, but to recognize and respect the differences that make the strength of the body of Christ.

sens: Lower part of the trunk, between the pelvis and the ribs
What one girds or encircles to prepare for action or service
Symbolic place of generative strength and descent
Inner seat of moral strength or stability
G3751.detail:
1. The loin is the lower part of the back, the flanks of the body (Matthew 3:4 and Mark 1:6: John the Baptist had a belt around his loins). It is an important area of the body that one girds or protects.
2. Girding the loins means preparing oneself, equipping oneself for action, as one lifts their robe to run or work (Luke 12:35: "Let your loins be girded"). It is an image of vigilance and readiness (Ephesians 6:14: wearing truth as a belt around the loins).
3. In Hebrew thought, the loins are the seat of life and generation: it is said that a person "is born from the loins" of an ancestor to express physical descent (Hebrews 7:5, 7:10: the Levites are from the loins of Abraham, meaning Abraham is their ancestor).
4. Figuratively, "girding one's loins" with virtue or truth means to strengthen oneself morally and spiritually for the Christian life (1 Peter 1:13: girding the loins of your mind).
G3751.origine: The Greek word ὀσφύς (osphus) literally refers to the region of the flanks and loins. In Hebrew, the word מֹתֶן (moten) that translates it has the same concrete and symbolic scope. The Hebrews saw the loins as the seat of vital power and procreative strength, which explains why the word takes on a figurative meaning to speak of descent and inheritance.
G3751.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the New Testament. First in the concrete sense: John the Baptist wears a belt around his loins (Matthew and Mark). Then in the figurative sense of preparation for action: "girding one's loins" to be ready, alert (Luke, Ephesians, 1 Peter). Finally, in the sense of descent: one speaks of someone who "is born from the loins" of an ancestor to signify heredity (Hebrews). Acts 2:30 also mentions the fruit of the loins (the descent of the Christ promised to David).
G3751.portee: This word teaches us how the Bible uses the body to speak of spiritual dispositions. "Girding one's loins" invites the Christian to actively prepare, with vigilance and strength, for the life of faith. It is a call to sobriety and availability to God. Moreover, seeing the loins as the seat of life reminds us that our physical existence is linked to our spiritual responsibility.

sens: At what time, under what circumstance
Whenever, every time that
At the moment when, as soon as
If ever, in case that
As long as, for as long as
G3752.detail:
1. The most direct meaning: to ask or indicate a specific moment in time. "When the hour comes, you will remember" (John 16:4) — it is a future moment, well-defined although one does not know exactly when.
2. Whenever an action is repeated: "When the unclean spirits saw him, they fell down before him" (Mark 3:11) — it was regular, habitual, at every encounter.
3. The immediate moment when two things coincide: "When they fail you" (Luke 16:9) — it is the moment when one follows the other without delay.
4. A condition subject to chance or uncertainty: "When I am weak, then I am strong" (2 Corinthians 12:10) — it is a truth that applies as long as weakness persists.
5. Introducing a hypothetical future thought, what "should" happen: "Blessed are you when they revile you" (Matthew 5:11) — the moment is expected, not yet here, but certain to come.
G3752.origine: The Greek word comes from the fusion of « ὅτε » (« when ») and « ἄν » (the particle of condition and uncertainty). This combination creates a nuance: not a fixed moment, but an expected, hypothetical moment that will occur one day. It is a frequent word in classical Greek and in Homer to speak of what happens regularly or what is to come.
G3752.emploi: This word appears about 120 times in the New Testament, especially in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) and the Epistles. It most often expresses the temporal subordination of one action to another: "When the master of the house comes..." (Mark 14:25: "I will not drink again until the day when I drink it new"). Sometimes it marks habit or repetition (Mark 3:11). Rarely, it may follow the indicative instead of the subjunctive (already visible in Mark 3:11 with the imperfect). The context shows whether it is an expected future, a habitual repetition, or a punctual moment.
G3752.portee: This word invites the reader to place their faith in a timeline of God. The promises of Jesus introduced by "when" are never vague: "When you are persecuted, you will be blessed" (Matthew 5:11). It is a word of hope and certainty — the moment will come, even if it is hidden. For the believer, it reminds us that trials and blessings come according to God's design, and we must hold on until that day.

sens: At the moment when, at the instant something occurs
Whenever, every time that
At the moment when a past action is fulfilled (since, once)
At the time when, while
In the future, on the day when
Indicating a relationship of place or circumstance (where)
G3753.detail:
1. When marks the precise moment when an event occurs: "After Jesus had finished these sayings" (Matthew 7:28) shows the endpoint of an action in the past that triggers a new fact. "When he was alone" (Mark 4:10) designates the instant when the disciples find themselves alone with Jesus.
2. The word also expresses repetition or habit: an action that occurs regularly or every time a condition is met, like a returning circumstance.
3. "Since" or "once": when the past action serves as the starting point of a new situation, notably with the perfect or imperfect — "we were exposed to tribulations, as it happened" (1 Thessalonians 3:4) shows the completed past that explains the present.
4. When situates a duration or context in time: "when we were with you" speaks of a whole period, not an isolated instant.
5. "The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in parables" (John 16:25) places a certain future event, a defined moment in God's plan.
6. "Days will come when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man" (Luke 17:22) or "where" relative: the word can simply mark the context, the state of affairs, or the place (value close to a location or circumstance).
G3753.origine: When comes from the Greek ὅτε (hote), which is the determined temporal form, correlating with πότε (pote, "when?"). Its basic image is that of a defined moment or time, as opposed to ὅταν (hotan), which expresses rather an indefinite or repeated condition. In Greek, ὅτε is regularly used with the indicative to fix a moment in the past, present, or concrete future.
G3753.emploi: When is one of the most frequent words in the New Testament (105 occurrences) and serves to structure the narrative. It appears mainly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) to introduce scenes or episodes: "After Jesus had finished these sayings" (Matthew 7:28) or "When he entered Capernaum" (Mark 1:32). When often accompanies the aorist (simple past tense) to mark a completed punctual event, but also the imperfect for a past circumstance ("when we were with you"), the present for an ongoing action, or very rarely the future for a certain upcoming moment (John 16:25). In Acts and in the epistles, when structures the narration or reasoning. The word can also take on a relative or circumstantial value ("where"), especially when a time noun precedes it.
G3753.portee: For the reader, when anchors the words and actions of Jesus in concrete moments: it gives weight to the story and shows that the Gospel is not an abstract doctrine but real, situated events that unfold according to the time and will of God. Recognizing the moment of a word or promise helps to grasp its meaning and significance. Finally, when also marks God's timelines: the future promises announced to the disciples ("The hour is coming when") place them in active trust, as they are inscribed in the divine plan.

sens: Introduces a complement clause after a verb of perception, knowledge, or speech (what one sees, knows, says, thinks)
Introduces a clause that defines or explains a person or thing designated by a demonstrative pronoun
Introduces reported direct speech (often untranslatable in French)
Expresses cause or reason (because, for)
G3754G.detail:
1. After verbs of seeing, knowing, thinking, saying, feeling, "that" introduces what is the object of these actions: what is perceived or communicated. Example: "Herod, seeing that he had been tricked by the Magi, became very angry" (Matthew 2:16) — here we see that "that" connects to "seeing" the reported information. Or again: "I know that this will turn out for my deliverance" (Philippians 1:19) — this is what we know.
2. After the verb "to be" (or "to become"), "that" explains what a person or thing truly is, often in response to an implicit question. Example: "He declared that he was not the Christ" (John 1:20) — this answers the question "Who are you?"
3. Sometimes "that" introduces direct speech without really being translated: modern French omits it. Example: "Mark 9:13 — I tell you that Elijah has come" where French could also say "I tell you: Elijah has come."
4. "That" also expresses cause or reason: "because, for." Example: "We rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces perseverance" (Romans 5:3) — suffering glorifies us because it produces perseverance.
G3754G.origine: The Greek word ὅτι comes from ὅστις ("he who, whoever"), retaining its neuter form. Originally, it was a neuter pronoun that designated a thing or idea; gradually, it became fixed as a simple logical linking tool. In Hebrew, the frequent equivalent is כִּי (kî), which also carries the meanings of "that" and "for." The versatility of the word reflects the absence, in both ancient Greek and Hebrew, of a strict distinction between these two functions: saying and causing are intertwined in the same logic of explanation.
G3754G.emploi: The word ὅτι is one of the most frequent in the New Testament (over 800 occurrences). It appears in almost every book. Its major uses are: (1) after verbs of knowledge, perception, or speech: "I see that," "I know that," "I say that" (very common in the four Gospels); (2) after "to be" to define an identity or nature; (3) before reported speech, where modern French tends to omit it; (4) to express cause or reason, particularly in the epistles (1 John, Romans). Its function varies according to context, but it always serves to link an act of thought, speech, or reason to its content.
G3754G.portee: This small word is the framework of biblical thought: it connects what we believe, what we know, what we say to its foundation or justification. For the Christian reader, understanding the uses of "that" helps to see how the apostles support their faith: not through isolated statements, but by chaining cause and effect, vision and its interpretation. This invites one not to settle for hearing a declaration, but to follow the movement of reason that supports it.

sens: Introduces an explanation or reason: explains why something has happened or is true
Introduces the content of an assertion or knowledge: what one asserts, thinks, or knows
Introduces reported direct speech: marks the beginning of someone's words
G3754H.detail:
1. When one wants to explain why something happens, one says "for" followed by the reason. For example, in Matthew 5:3, Jesus says, "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven": "for" explains why these people are blessed. Or again John 1:17: "for the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ": this is a justification of what has just been said.
2. After verbs that express thought or speech (believe, know, say, see), "for" introduces what one thinks or asserts. For example, in Luke 4:6, the devil says: "I will give you all this authority... for it has been given to me." Here "for" does not really explain a cause, but exposes the content of his assertion.
3. Sometimes "for" appears at the beginning of reported speech without there being really a causality: it is just the Greek way of marking that one is reporting direct words. This word is then difficult to translate into French.
G3754H.origine: The word "hoti" comes from ancient Greek and originates from a relative interrogative pronoun "hostis" (who, whoever). It has grammaticalized to become a very common conjunction that links clauses. In Greek, it is one of the main tools for structuring a complex sentence and marking logical relationships between ideas. It has no direct equivalent in biblical Hebrew: different prepositions or conjunctions (depending on the context) played this role in the Old Testament.
G3754H.emploi: "Hoti" is the most frequent Greek word in the New Testament (over 440 times). It appears in all books and is mainly used in three ways: first to express a cause or reason ("for," "because"), very common in the beatitudes of Matthew 5 or in Paul's teachings; secondly after verbs of thought and speech to introduce what one believes or says ("that," often invisible in French); finally to introduce reported speech. Depending on translations and contexts, it is rendered as "for," "because," "that," or nothing at all. It is a versatile conjunction, which French must adapt to each occurrence to remain natural.
G3754H.portee: Knowing this word allows one to better follow the logic of a biblical sentence: one sees which assertions are linked and why. When Jesus or Paul say "for" something, one immediately understands that what follows is an explanation, proof, or justification of what precedes. It is a guide for reading attentively and grasping how the Bible structures its arguments and revelations.

sens: Negation particle indicating the absence or refusal of an action or state
Direct response 'no' to reject an assertion
Emphasis of strong refusal or prohibition when associated with other particles
Ironically softened expression where negation reinforces affirmation (litotes)
G3756.detail:
1. The Greek particle "ou" (or "ouk" before a soft vowel, "ouch" before a hard vowel) denies a real fact or action. It is the negation of the real, of what is observed. It is often accompanied by a verb in the indicative: "Joseph did not know his wife until she had borne a son" (Matthew 1:25) or "the two shall become one flesh; so they are no longer two" (Mark 10:8).

2. Used alone or emphasized by accent, it directly answers 'no' to a question: "Are you Elijah? He said: I am not" (John 1:21).

3. Combined with other negative particles (notably "mê"), it reinforces prohibition or creates a double negation that astonishes: the prohibition then becomes absolute and serious, like a divine prohibition.

4. In ironic language (what is called a litote), the negation paradoxically accentuates an affirmation: saying "he is not an insignificant man" (Acts 21:39) means "he is an important man." Saying "they did not find few" (Acts 17:4) means "they found many."
G3756.origine: The Greek word "ou" translates the Hebrew negations "lo" and "aïn." It comes from a very ancient root common to Indo-European languages. Its form changes according to the sound that follows ("ouk" before a soft vowel, "ouch" before a hard vowel) to smooth pronunciation, which Greek grammarians called euphony. It is the negation of objective reality, unlike "mê" which expresses a subjective negation or prohibition.
G3756.emploi: This particle is one of the most frequent in the New Testament: it appears about 1,446 times. It is found everywhere, in all books and contexts. It denies established facts ("Joseph did not know her"), contradicts assumptions ("These men are not drunk"), rejects assertions ("This is not his intention"). It can deny a unique past or present action, but also express a general law: "No one can serve two masters." It constantly combines with other words for nuance: with another "ou" to reinforce, with "allá" (but) to present an alternative, with "mê" to create a prohibition more serious than simple prohibition.
G3756.portee: For the Christian reader, this small particle is fundamental: it builds the understanding of the biblical message. It helps us to see clearly what Jesus refuses, what he denies, what he corrects in false knowledge. It also distinguishes the real fact (marked by "ou") from fear or doubt (marked by "mê"). Recognizing the strength and precision of these negations helps to grasp the teaching without distorting it.

sens: At what place, location (to ask or indicate a place)
To what place, in what direction (to indicate movement)
In a given situation, state, or condition (in a figurative sense)
G3757.detail:
1. "Where" poses or answers the question about location: "At what place?" It asks or shows precisely the physical location where something is or happens. For example, in Acts 1:13, the disciples gather in "the upper room, where" they were staying — this is the concrete place where they were assembled.

2. "Where" also indicates movement toward a place: "To what place?" or "In what place are we going?" This is the sense of movement, of direction taken. In Luke 10:1, Jesus sends his disciples "to all the places where he himself was to go" — they are going toward those places.

3. "Where" is also used for an abstract situation or condition, without physical movement: it is the context in which something is found. In Romans 5:20, Paul writes "Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more" — "where" describes the situation of sin, not a geographical location.
G3757.origine: This word comes from classical Greek and derives from the relative "who, that" used adverbially to indicate place. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it often corresponds to words like "sham" (there) or "an" (where), which also carried this dual meaning of place and direction. The Greek word has retained this flexibility: it works both to ask for a place and to indicate it or to express a condition.
G3757.emploi: This word appears 25 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. It serves three main roles: first, it localizes events (Matthew 2:9, "the star went and stood over the place where the child was"), then it indicates a destination (Luke 24:28, "he acted as if he were going farther"), finally it describes a moral or spiritual condition (Romans 5:20, "where sin increased"). Its meaning adjusts to the context: when it follows a verb of movement (go, come, send), it answers "where?"; when it introduces a general situation, it functions as "where" or "in which."
G3757.portee: This small word reminds us that God knows all the places we go and where we are. It also helps us understand that biblical events are never floating in the abstract: they happen somewhere, at a specific place. Finally, when Paul speaks of "where sin abounds," he shows us that God's grace is never absent from our difficult situations.

sens: Exclamation of call or mockery
Expression of surprise or irony
Cry intended to attract attention
G3758.detail:
1. It is an interjection, a spontaneous cry, not a constructed phrase. It expresses astonishment, indignation, or mockery depending on the context. In Mark 15:29, the passersby cry "Hey!" mocking the crucified Jesus, as if to say: "Look at him!" or "Well now!" — it is a cry of derision.
2. The interjection can also mark irony: the speaker feigns surprise or admiration to belittle or ridicule someone. The insults that follow ("you who destroy the temple") confirm that this "Hey" is not friendly, but contemptuous.
3. More broadly, it is a cry to hail, call, attract attention — like saying "Hey, you!" to address someone.
G3758.origine: It is a simple and universal interjection, common to many ancient languages. It does not come from a grammatical root, but is a natural cry, a sound produced by the voice to express emotion or call. It is a purely expressive word, very ancient.
G3758.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 15:29. It is a dramatic detail of the Passion narrative: the passersby witnessing the crucifixion of Jesus cry "Hey!" in a mocking manner, accompanying their cry with gestures of derision (shaking their heads) and insults ("you who destroy the temple"). This interjection paints the hostility and contempt of the moment.
G3758.portee: This exclamation reminds us of the concrete humiliation that Jesus endured: not just a silent condemnation, but the cries and mockery of the crowd. It invites us to measure what Christ suffered for us, even in these brutal and human details.

sens: exclamation of mourning or pity in the face of calamity
prophetic condemnation addressed to one who acts wickedly or rejects God
announcement of divine judgment on a city, group, or individual
expression of lamentation over a dire or inevitable fate
G3759.detail:
1. Woe is an exclamation of deep affliction, comparable to a cry of distress in the face of suffering. Jesus uses it with compassion: "Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!" (Matthew 11:21) expresses both sadness and the seriousness of their refusal to believe.

2. It is also a word of prophetic judgment directed against those who commit injustice or hypocrisy. The seven "woes" of Matthew 23 target the scribes and Pharisees: "Woe to you, scribes and hypocritical Pharisees!" (Matthew 23:23) denounces their moral unfaithfulness despite their apparent piety.

3. Woe signifies the punishment or calamity that will inevitably fall upon one who rejects God's message. "Woe to the one through whom [the scandals] come!" (Luke 17:1) shows that this word announces an unavoidable judgment.

4. It also expresses lamentation in the face of terrible circumstances or certain guilt. "Woe to those who are pregnant in those days" (Mark 13:17) evokes future suffering, and "Woe to the one who delivers the Son of Man!" (Mark 14:21) proclaims the tragic fate of Judas.
G3759.origine: The Greek word ouai renders the Hebrew hoi (הוֹי), an ancient interjection expressing mourning or alarm. This exclamation belonged to the language of the prophets of the Old Testament, who cried "hoi" to announce God's judgment on Israel and the nations. Jesus takes up this traditional prophetic form, but imbues it with a new authority: these are no longer just words of condemnation, but the voice of the Son of God himself.
G3759.emploi: The word ouai appears 36 times in the New Testament, primarily in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) and Revelation. Matthew uses it 13 times, notably in the series of seven rebukes against the Pharisees (chapter 23). Luke often places it in the mouth of Jesus in situations of contrast or rupture, particularly in the Sermon on the Plain (Luke 6:24-26) where he contrasts the "woes" with the "beatitudes." Mark uses it for announcements of eschatological calamity (13:17, 14:21). Revelation uses it solemnly to mark successive divine judgments (9:12, 11:14, 18:10, 18:16). In 1 Corinthians 9:16, Paul uses it metaphorically: "Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel!", expressing an unavoidable obligation.
G3759.portee: This word reminds the reader that there is a moral responsibility before God: the refusal to obey, hypocrisy, and injustice do not go unnoticed. But it is also a final warning, an invitation to repent before judgment comes. In hearing "woe," one is called to see where true justice and true life are found, which is offered only by the Gospel.

sens: In no way, absolutely not
By no means, no one could
Of all certainty, without the slightest doubt
G3760.detail:
1. The word expresses an absolute and energetic negation: something is truly, genuinely not the case. It is an unequivocal refusal of what one might think or fear. In Matthew 2:6, when it is said that Bethlehem is "certainly not" the least of the cities of Judah, it asserts with certainty that it is not small or insignificant in any way — on the contrary, it is great and glorious.
2. The meaning can also emphasize that by no means, no force in the world could contradict what is being asserted. It reinforces the absolute impossibility.
3. In certain contexts, "certainly" also carries the idea of certain confirmation: one asserts something in an indisputable manner.
G3760.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "not one" (a combination of negation particles: οὐ- "no" and -δαμός "any"). It thus expresses total absence, the exclusion of any exception. It is a classical Greek adverb formed to give negation extreme and solemn force.
G3760.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 2:6, in a quotation from the Old Testament (Micah 5:2). It is found in a prophetic and solemn context: it asserts that Bethlehem, despite its modest appearance, will absolutely not be insignificant, for the Messiah will come from it. The unique and solemn use of this adverb underscores the absolute significance of this messianic assertion.
G3760.portee: This word invites the reader to perceive the certainty with which Scripture affirms its truths, particularly those concerning the Messiah and the divine plan. Bethlehem is only small in appearance: God will bring forth the Savior of the world from it. The word reminds us that the realities of God transcend our human evaluations.

sens: coordinating negative conjunction: "and not", "neither"
introducing a second negation in a sentence: "not either"
reinforcing complete absence: "not even"
G3761.detail:
1. This word is a negative conjunction that links two elements by denying both. It is used to say "and not" or "neither", as in Matthew 25:13: "Therefore keep watch, because you do not know either the day or the hour" — both are unknown at the same time.
2. It introduces a second negation coordinated with the first, to continue the negative thought. In John 14:17, the Spirit is described as one whom the world "does not see and does not know": the double negation emphasizes the total inability of the world.
3. When it appears alone or with an accusative, it can reinforce the absolute nature of the negation: "not even". In Luke 12:26, Jesus says, "If you cannot do even the least thing", where the word indicates that the impossible begins with small things.
G3761.origine: This Greek word comes from the root of negation (like "or" in French: "or... or"), enriched with a particle that adds the meaning of "also", "and". It corresponds in Hebrew to the word "gam-lô" ("and not") or to "al" ("not"). Structurally, it is to the negative what "kai" ("and") is to the positive: it coordinates by denying rather than affirming.
G3761.emploi: This word is very frequent in the New Testament (131 times), primarily as a coordinating negative conjunction in all the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) and in Acts and the epistles. It often appears after a first negation to add a second denied term ("neither... nor"), or alone to reinforce a negation ("not... not"). Its usage varies: sometimes it coordinates two nouns (day and hour in Matthew 25:13), sometimes two verbs or two propositions (see/know in John 14:17). In some cases, it nuances the scope of the negation by restricting or universalizing ("not even one").
G3761.portee: This simple yet omnipresent word reveals the rigor of biblical speech: the things not said are as important as those that are. When Jesus says that one cannot serve two masters "nor the one nor the other" fully, or that the Holy Spirit is neither seen nor known by the world, the double "nor" insists on absolute exclusivity. Learning to note these small words teaches the reader not to linger with the things of the world if they contradict the service of God.

sens: No human being, not a single one
G3762.detail: 1. The word denotes the total absence of persons or human beings. It expresses an absolute negation: "no one can serve two masters" (Matthew 6:24) means that no living being has this capacity. It is a universal statement of impossibility or absence.
G3762.origine: The Greek word οὐδείς is formed from the negation οὐ ("not") and a root meaning "one" or "someone." It is distinguished from its equivalent μηδείς by the type of negation: οὐδείς expresses an objective and real negation (what does not actually exist), while μηδείς expresses a subjective or conditional negation. The word covers any absence of a human person in the universe of discourse.
G3762.emploi: This word is one of the most frequent in the New Testament (222 occurrences). It appears in all the Gospels and in the epistles, particularly in Paul. It can denote the total absence of a person ("no one can work at night," John 9:4), serve to deny a universal capacity ("no one has seen God," John 1:18), or reinforce a negative statement ("Jesus answered him nothing," Luke 23:9, where "nothing" corresponds to the same root). Its usage varies from the strict sense (zero persons) to rhetorical uses that emphasize the universality of a negative assertion.
G3762.portee: For the reader, this word expresses absolute authority: when Jesus says "no one" can accomplish something, he establishes an unavoidable spiritual law. It also shows urgency ("no one can work at night") and invites seizing the divine opportunity. It is a word that reveals our human limits and the uniqueness of God alone.

sens: At no time in the past, present, or future
Under no circumstances, absolutely not
Not once
G3763.detail: 1. The word expresses the total absence of an event throughout all time — it has never happened, is not happening now, and will never happen. Jesus says to his disciples: "Never has man spoken like this man" (John 7:46), meaning that no one before him had ever expressed themselves in this way. 2. It also indicates an impossibility or absolute refusal: Peter asserts that Jesus will never be a stumbling block for him (Matthew 26:33), promising his unconditional faithfulness. 3. In a question, the word calls for reflection: "Have you never read what David did?" (Mark 2:25) asks the interlocutors if they truly know the Scriptures.
G3763.origine: The Greek word is composed of two elements: "οὐδέ" (which means "nor, not even") and "ποτε" (which means "one day, at any time"). This combination reinforces the idea of total and absolute negation. The word literally expresses "not even at any time."
G3763.emploi: The word appears 15 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels of Matthew and Mark, and in Acts. It is used to express definitive and solemn negations: Jesus declares that he never knows those who commit iniquity (Matthew 7:23), witnesses assert they have never seen anything like it (Mark 2:12). Peter protests that no unclean meat has ever entered his mouth (Acts 11:8). Paul writes that love never fails (1 Corinthians 13:8). The word is also used in rhetorical questions that invite meditation on the word of God.
G3763.portee: This word reminds us that certain realities are definitive and unchangeable. When Jesus says to someone, "I never knew you," it is a judgment that cannot be revoked. Conversely, when he says that the love of God never fails, it assures us of eternal faithfulness. The word helps us grasp the absolute importance of certain biblical truths.

sens: Indicates that an action or state has not yet occurred at the time of the narrative
Expresses an expectation: something is planned but has not been realized
Marks a temporal limitation: the moment has not arrived
G3764.detail: 1. The word simply denotes that something has not occurred up to the present. In John 7:39, the Holy Spirit had not yet been given to believers because Jesus had not yet been glorified — the moment was planned but had not come. In John 19:41, the tomb was new and no one had yet been laid there: no one had yet needed it. 2. The word marks a waiting stage, an event in the unfolding of God's plan. In John 20:9, the disciples did not yet understand that Jesus must rise from the dead: understanding was to come, and it would come. In Acts 8:16, the Spirit had not yet descended on the Samaritans, although water baptism had already taken place — two distinct stages. 3. It is a negation adverb combined with time: it emphasizes not an impossibility, but the absence of an action up to that precise moment in the narrative.
G3764.origine: The Greek word οὐδέπω comes from the combination of οὐ (negation) and δέ (particle meaning "and") and πώ (ever). It translates the Hebrew טֶרֶם (terem) which literally expresses the idea of "not yet." It is a negative time adverb that places the action outside the present and indicates that it is destined to occur.
G3764.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the New Testament, all in the Gospel of John or in Acts. It is used to mark a temporal stage that has not yet been crossed: the Holy Spirit not yet given, an event to come. John uses this word to emphasize that certain realities are inscribed in God's plan but whose time has not yet come. It is a narrative word that creates tension between the current moment and the prophesied future: it situates the reader at a precise moment in the history of salvation where something is pending.
G3764.portee: This word reminds us that the history of salvation unfolds according to God's timing, not ours. Many spiritual realities and divine promises do not arrive instantly: they are fulfilled according to a precise schedule. This invites the reader to see how the events of Scripture are progressively ordered — water baptism before receiving the Spirit, Christ's death before understanding the resurrection. Understanding "not yet" helps to live in the confidence that what is not yet will come.

sens: Marks a logical conclusion that follows from what precedes
Introduces a reply or question that responds to what has just been said
G3766.detail: 1. The word introduces a conclusion: what follows logically or naturally derives from the previous sentence. It is a chain of reasoning. When Pilate says to Jesus, "Are you therefore a king?" he draws this question from the affirmation he has just made or heard: it is the consequence of what precedes. 2. It can also mark a reply or an objection that extends the exchange. Pilate drives the point home, reformulating to confirm or confront Jesus with his own words. The "therefore" shows that the question bounces off what has just been stated.
G3766.origine: The Greek word οὐκοῦν is composed of the negative adverb οὔ (not) and a form of the interrogative adverb. Originally, it literally meant "is it not therefore?" or "is it not then?" Over time, the negative element faded from the meaning, and the word retained only the idea of consequence and logical connection. It is a common tool of Greek dialectic.
G3766.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 18:37, at the moment when Pilate interrogates Jesus. Pilate, confronted with the statements he has just heard, logically draws a question: "Are you therefore a king?" The word marks the connection between what has been said and the question that arises. In this judicial context, the "therefore" gives weight to the interrogation: Pilate links his question to the reality being reported to him.
G3766.portee: This word shows us how truth is expressed through logical connection. Jesus declares that he came to bear witness to the truth; Pilate naturally draws the question, "Are you a king?" This connection reminds us that faith does not ignore reason: what Jesus says is coherent and calls for a thoughtful response. Pilate's "therefore" invites us to follow the thread of reasoning in light of the revelation.

sens: Expresses a logical consequence: what naturally follows from what precedes
Introduces an exhortation or a call to action based on what has just been said
Poses a question that logically follows from the previous statement
Resumes or continues a narrative after a pause or digression
Marks a simple succession of ideas or events without strict causal link
G3767.detail:
1. The word expresses that one thing naturally follows another, like a conclusion. For example, in Romans 3:27, Paul asks: "Where then is boasting?" — this is a question that logically follows from his previous argument about justification by faith.

2. In exhortations, it reinforces a command by grounding it in what precedes: "Be merciful, therefore, just as your Father is merciful" (Luke 6:36) means "since God is merciful, you must be too."

3. Often it introduces a question that arises from the previous statement, as in Matthew 22:43: "How then does David call him Lord?" — the question logically follows from what has just been posed.

4. The word can also simply resume an interrupted narrative thread or continue a story, without expressing a true logical consequence. In Matthew 1:17, "Thus there were fourteen generations in all" resumes the genealogical thread after enumeration.

5. Sometimes "therefore" marks just a transition or a light link between two ideas, almost a simple punctuation of speech: it says "and so?" rather than "and consequently."
G3767.origine: The Greek word oun is a very common particle that does not relate to any specific root: it is a discourse tool, a connector. In Hebrew, words like לָכֵן (lakhen, "therefore") or phrases like וַיְהִי ("and it came to pass") play similar roles. Oun does not come from a concrete image, but from the need of speakers to logically or simply connect their thoughts. It is a word of remarkable stability: it has hardly changed in meaning or function from classical Greek to New Testament Greek.
G3767.emploi: The word therefore (oun) is one of the most frequent in the New Testament: it appears 526 times. It never occupies the first position in a sentence — this is a strict rule. It mainly serves to link consecutive ideas, particularly in John, who uses it very often to continue his narrative. In the Gospels, it is also found in questions ("How therefore?", "Why therefore?") and in exhortations (commands or advice supported by a "therefore"). In Romans and the epistles, it structures logical arguments: Paul uses it to show that his conclusions derive from his premises. Sometimes it accompanies a participle or a conjunction (as in Acts 2:30 or Romans 5:1) to reinforce the causal link.
G3767.portee: This small word teaches the reader to think logically in faith: each "therefore" in Scripture invites us to follow divine reasoning, to see how God's grace produces concrete obedience, or how the knowledge of a truth must transform our lives. In exhortations, "be merciful therefore" reminds us that our moral duty always rests on God's character or on what He has done. It is a word that teaches us not to separate doctrine from practice: the biblical "therefore" always links one to the other.

sens: Indicates that an action or moment has not yet occurred, that a state does not exist at a given moment in the narrative
Indicates an expectation, a delay before something happens or the time arrives
In the interrogative or negative form, marks doubt, astonishment, or reproach at the absence of understanding or progress
G3768.detail:
1. The word simply designates what has not yet occurred. It is a marker in time: at this moment in the narrative, an action remains future or a state does not yet exist. When Jesus says to his mother, "My hour has not yet come" (John 2:4), he means that the moment he is waiting for has not started, even though the feast continues.

2. The word expresses the idea of an expectation, a delay to come. It sets the future horizon: something will come, but not now. "I am not going up, because my time has not yet fully come" (John 7:8): Jesus is waiting for a moment set by his Father before going down to Jerusalem.

3. Used in a question or in a negative construction, the word carries a nuance of tender reproach or astonishment: "Do you not yet understand?" (Mark 8:21) asks the disciples why, after so many miracles and teachings, understanding has not taken root in them. It is an invitation to progress.
G3768.origine: The word is composed of the negation οὐ (ou) — which simply denies a fact — and a temporal particle πω (pō) that reinforces the idea of delay or limit. This construction marks a negation situated in time: not an absolute negation (like "never"), but a transitional negation ("not yet"). In Hebrew and Aramaic, the idea was often expressed by a negation associated with a verb of time.
G3768.emploi: The word appears 26 times in the New Testament, notably in John (8 occurrences), in the Synoptic Gospels, and a few times in Paul and Revelation. It is common to mark the present moment of the narrative — a future action — in the speeches of Jesus and spiritual reflections. In John, it often serves to indicate that Jesus' hour has not yet come, or that the knowledge of God has not yet been acquired. In the disciples' questions ("Are you still without understanding?" Matthew 16:9), it expresses astonishment at their lack of faith or understanding, giving a tone of tender pedagogy. Revelation uses it to speak of future time: "five have fallen; one is, the other has not yet come" (Revelation 17:10).
G3768.portee: This word invites the believer to enter into the dynamic of waiting and trust. When Jesus says, "My hour has not yet come," he teaches that God leads events according to a right moment, not according to haste. For the reader of the Gospel, "not yet" is a reminder that the fullness of the knowledge of God in Christ comes gradually and that the disciples, like us, never grasp everything at once. It is a word that places patience and humility at the heart of faith.

sens: Elongated appendage located at the back of an animal's body
Extension or trail of something that stretches
Instrument of power or action in a symbolic vision
G3769.detail:
1. The tail is the fleshy appendage that extends the body of certain animals, such as in scorpions or snakes. In Revelation 9:10, the infernal creatures have "tails like scorpions and stingers," a concrete image of a venomous and stinging threat.
2. The tail can also refer to what drags, what stretches behind: in Revelation 12:4, the "tail" of the dragon "swept away a third of the stars of heaven," an image of destructive force that carries everything in its path.
3. In John's visions, the tail becomes an instrument of power and harmful action. In Revelation 9:19, the power of the infernal creatures resides "in their mouths and in their tails": the tail is thus an active vector of destruction and evil, a spiritual weapon.
G3769.origine: The Greek word οὐρά comes from an Indo-European root meaning the back, what drags. The Hebrew זָנָב (zanab) has the same concrete meaning. In the ancient Greek Bible, this word regularly translates this Hebrew term. The image is simple and universal: the tail is what extends the body backward, often with a connotation of movement or power.
G3769.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in the Revelation of John. It is never used in the literal sense to describe an ordinary animal, but always in symbolic or apocalyptic visions. In Revelation 9:10 and 9:19, the tail is an element of terror: it carries venom, the power to strike. In Revelation 12:4, it becomes an instrument of cosmic destruction, sweeping away the stars. Each time, the tail embodies an active threat, a hostile power directed against men or heaven.
G3769.portee: For the reader of Revelation, the "tail" reminds us that evil does not only manifest through what is visible on the surface, but through what drags behind, what pulls, what prolongs destruction. It is an invitation to see beyond appearances and to recognize that the hostile powers against God act through multiple and insidious means, like a tail that strikes by surprise.

sens: Belonging to heaven, to the dwelling place of God
Coming from God or His domain
Surpassing earthly and human limits
Divine or of divine essence
G3770.detail:
1. The word describes what belongs to heaven, the eternal domain where God dwells: for example, "your heavenly Father" (Matthew 5:48) refers to God as He sits in heaven and reigns over creation from there. It is the adjective that establishes the contrast between heaven and earth.
2. It also qualifies what emanates from God or proceeds from His divine authority: when Jesus says, "Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted" (Matthew 15:13), He speaks of what has received the approval and order of God Himself.
3. The word also carries a nuance of perfection and transcendence: by saying, "Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect" (Matthew 5:48), Jesus invites His disciples to imitate a holiness that surpasses what humans can achieve on their own.
4. Finally, it expresses the divine character and eternal essence: an army of believers who praise God in Luke 2:13 is called heavenly because it participates in the divine and eternal world.
G3770.origine: The word comes from the Greek « ouranos » which means heaven, the visible firmament, and takes here the form of an adjective indicating what belongs to or relates to heaven. In Hebrew, the Old Testament Greek often translates the word « shamayim » (שָׁמַיִם) with this term, which refers to both the physical firmament and the seat of divinity. The Greek suffix adds the idea of belonging or relation: to be heavenly is to be of the domain of heaven.
G3770.emploi: The word appears nine times in the New Testament, only in the Gospels and Acts. Matthew uses it seven times, almost exclusively in the context of Jesus' teaching, to qualify "the Father": in Matthew 5:48, 6:14, 6:26, 6:32, 15:13, 18:35, and 23:9. This repetition emphasizes that the Father Jesus speaks of is not an earthly father, but God Himself, who sits in heaven and acts from heaven. Luke uses the word in 2:13 for the multitude of the heavenly host who sings the glory of God, while in Acts 26:19, Paul says he obeyed the heavenly vision, meaning the order that came from the divine domain. The word thus reinforces the idea that what is being discussed pertains to divine authority, wisdom, and perfection.
G3770.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize that God reigns from above and that His life, will, and perfection transcend our earthly understanding. When Jesus speaks of "your heavenly Father," He creates a paradoxical intimacy: God is both distant and infinitely close, sovereign and benevolent. This word also helps the disciple to lift his gaze beyond material and temporal concerns to align with the values of the kingdom of God.

sens: From the heavenly region, from where rain and light come
Sent or manifested by God from on high
G3771.detail:
1. The word literally designates what comes from the heavenly region, the heaven where God and His creatures reside. In Acts 14:17, Paul speaks of the rains and fruitful seasons that come down from heaven: it is the image of heaven as the source of the material blessings that God grants to humanity.
2. The word can also express a divine action or manifestation: in Acts 26:13, the light that shines "from heaven" is a direct intervention from God, a heavenly vision that surpasses the light of the sun. It is heaven viewed as the seat of God and the supernatural.
G3771.origine: The Greek word οὐρανόθεν (ouranothen) is formed from οὐρανός (ouranos), which means "heaven" or "firmament," to which is added the suffix -θεν (-then) indicating provenance or origin ("from where"). It is like adding "from" to "heaven." The word belongs to the Greek family of the adjective and noun "ouranos" which regularly translates the Hebrew שָׁמַיִם (shamayim), heaven as the space created by God and the seat of His presence.
G3771.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the Acts of the Apostles. In Acts 14:17, in Paul's speech at Lystra, he mentions the heavenly benefits — rains and fruits — that God continuously distributes to all peoples. In Acts 26:13, in the account of his conversion, Paul describes the extraordinary light that shone around him and his companions: a light of heavenly origin, a manifestation of God's presence. In both cases, the word emphasizes the divine or heavenly origin of the phenomenon described.
G3771.portee: This word reminds us that God remains the master of heaven and earth, the source of all good gifts. It helps the reader to see in natural phenomena — rains, seasons — signs of God's care. It also reinforces the reality of divine visions or interventions: when something comes "from heaven," it is God Himself who acts and manifests to His people.

sens: the visible space above the earth, where clouds, the sun, the moon, and stars are seen
the universe or the whole world (heaven and earth combined)
the dwelling place of God, angels, and blessed beings
by allusion, God himself or his will (a discreet way of referring to him)
the kingship or reign of God
G3772.detail:
1. Heaven is primarily what we see: the blue or cloudy expanse above our heads, with its celestial bodies. We speak of the red of the sky (Matthew 16:3), stars falling from heaven (Mark 13:25), or birds of heaven that feed (Matthew 6:26).

2. Sometimes the word refers not only to the visible space but to the entire universe — heaven and earth together. Thus, "heaven and earth will pass away" (Matthew 5:18, 24:35) means that all creation will disappear.

3. Heaven is also the place where God dwells, where angels reign, and where the glorified Christ has sat. Jesus tells his disciples that there is a building for us in heaven (2 Corinthians 5:1), a treasure in heaven (Matthew 6:20).

4. By a very common figure, especially in Matthew, "heaven" becomes a respectful way to refer to God himself, without naming him directly. This is a Jewish habit: one says, "heaven has permitted" rather than "God has permitted" (Matthew 21:25).

5. The expression "the kingdom of heaven" means the reign of God or his kingship. To say that this reign is "near" (Matthew 3:2) is to announce that God will govern in a new way through Jesus.
G3772.origine: The Greek word ouranos comes from an Indo-European root meaning "to cover" or "to envelop" — the heaven that covers the earth. In Hebrew, the equivalent word is shamayim ("heavens"), which gives its image to the Greek of the New Testament. The plural, often found in Greek ("the heavens"), reflects this Hebrew habit. When speaking of "the kingdom of heaven," it directly takes the Aramaic form used by Jesus and the masters of Israel.
G3772.emploi: The word appears 261 times in the New Testament, especially in Matthew (who uses it 82 times). In Matthew, the expression "the kingdom of heaven" is the usual formula of Jesus (Matthew 3:2, 4:17, 5:3, etc.). Mark and Luke prefer "the kingdom of God." The word "heaven" alone sometimes refers to the physical heaven (the stars, the clouds), sometimes to the dwelling place of God. Sometimes it relates to cosmic signs (Matthew 24:29: "the stars will fall from heaven"), sometimes to God himself (Matthew 5:34: "swear by heaven" = swear by God). In John 3:13, Jesus asserts that he descends from heaven and ascends there: it is heaven as the place of his divine glory.
G3772.portee: For the Christian reader, the word "heaven" reminds us that God exists beyond the visible, that he is master of all. When we pray "Our Father who art in heaven," we acknowledge his authority and holiness. The "kingdom of heaven" announces a new reality: God already reigns through Jesus, even if this reign must be fully realized at the end. This encourages the believer to seek first this kingdom (Matthew 6:33), rather than earthly riches.

sens: Disciple of Christ and co-worker of Paul in ministry
G3773.detail: Urban is a Christian mentioned only once in the Bible, in Paul's letter to the Romans. Paul greets him as his "fellow worker in Christ," which means he worked with Paul to spread the Gospel. It is an honor to receive such a mention in an apostolic epistle.
G3773.origine: The name Urbanus comes from Latin and literally means "of the city" or "urban." It is a common name in the Roman Empire. The Segond has Frenchified it to "Urbain." Nothing is known about his precise family or geographical origins.
G3773.emploi: Urban appears only once in Scripture, in Romans 16:9. Paul includes him among the Roman Christians he greets at the end of his letter. The context shows that he was an active worker in the early Church, working alongside the apostle. His name appears in a list of faithful individuals who deserved to be honored for their service.
G3773.portee: Urban reminds us that the early Church was populated by ordinary disciples whose names have been preserved by God's grace. His mention suggests that all faithful work for the Gospel, even that of lesser-known believers, is valued by the Lord and worth remembering.
