sens: Military officer in the service of King David
G3774.detail: Uriah is a soldier in King David's army. He is known as the husband of Bathsheba, the woman whom David coveted and with whom he had a son, Solomon, who became the famous king of Israel (Matthew 1:6).
G3774.origine: The Hebrew name אוּרִיָּה (Uriah) literally means "Yahweh is my light" or "God is my light." The word ור (or) means "light," and יה (Yah) is the abbreviated divine name. It is a typical theophoric name of the ancient Near East, where the proper name contained a confession of faith in the deity.
G3774.emploi: Uriah appears only once by name in the New Testament, in Matthew 1:6, in the genealogy of Jesus. Matthew mentions him as the husband of Bathsheba, the mother of Solomon. This reference points to the well-known account in the Old Testament (2 Samuel 11-12), where Uriah, officer of David's armies, dies in battle after David coveted his wife. Although Uriah is only mentioned once here, his presence in the genealogy of Jesus reminds us of God's grace toward David despite his grave sin.
G3774.portee: The mention of Uriah in the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew 1 shows that God omits no link in the history of salvation, even those marked by human sin. It reveals that the redemption of Jesus is woven into a real, complex story, where God acts despite and through the weaknesses of men. It is an invitation to hope in divine mercy.

sens: Auditory organ of the human body
Act of listening, perceiving by hearing
Personal attention, willingness to hear
Spiritual capacity to understand and obey God
Collective of those who listen
G3775.detail:
1. The ear is the physical organ with which sounds are heard (Luke 22:50: Peter cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant; Mark 7:33: Jesus puts his fingers in the ears of a deaf-mute). It is the body part intended to receive the word.

2. Having ears to hear means being able to listen and perceive (Mark 8:18: "Having ears, do you not hear?"). It is the concrete action of receiving a message through hearing.

3. "To the ear" means in secret, directly, and personally (Matthew 10:27: "What I tell you in the dark, speak in the light"). The ear represents the personal relationship between the speaker and the listener.

4. "He who has ears to hear" is a spiritual invitation to truly understand and put into practice the word of God (Matthew 13:43: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear"). It is less about the physical organ and more about the willingness to grasp the deeper meaning and obey it.

5. "The ears of the Lord" or "to reach the ears" refers to God's attentive listening, His knowledge of what is being said (James 5:4: "the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord"). This shows that God hears and welcomes the prayers of His children.
G3775.origine: The Greek word "ous" (ὦτος in the genitive) comes from a common Indo-European root in ancient languages to designate the auditory organ. In Hebrew, the corresponding word is "azen" (אֹזֶן), which shares the same etymological family. The notion of ear quickly became enriched: beyond the physical organ, it symbolizes obedience and the disposition of the heart to hear God's voice, as in ancient Semitic culture where "azen" could also mean "to obey" or "to listen attentively."
G3775.emploi: The word appears about 35 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. It is first used in the physical sense: John cuts off the ear of a servant (Luke 22:50), Jesus heals a deaf-mute (Mark 7:33). But very quickly, the ear becomes the image of spiritual receptivity. The phrase "He who has ears to hear, let him hear" recurs ten times or more (Matthew 11:15, 13:9, 13:43; Mark 4:9, 4:23; Luke 8:8, 14:35; Revelation 2:7, 2:11, 2:17, 2:29, 3:6, 3:13, 3:22, 13:9). It calls everyone to active and transformative listening. The expression "to the ear" (secret, personal) emphasizes the intimacy of the transmission (Matthew 10:27, Luke 12:3). Finally, "to reach the ears" marks the certainty that God hears the cries of His children (Acts 11:22, James 5:4).
G3775.portee: The ear in the Bible is not just a sensitive organ: it is the symbol of obedience and faith. Having ears to hear means preparing one's heart to receive the word of God, to trust it, and to put it into practice. For today's Christian, this word reminds us of the importance of active listening in prayer and in Bible reading: not merely passive hearing, but engaged attention, a willingness to let God speak and to respond. It is also an assurance: our prayers, our cries rise to the ears of the Lord, who listens to us with personal and loving attention.

sens: Property, wealth, material possession
Capital or inheritance owned by a family
What can be squandered or lost through mismanagement
G3776.detail:
1. The word concretely designates property, wealth, or the entirety of material goods that a person possesses. It constitutes one's heritage: in the parable of the prodigal son, the father "divided his goods" between his two sons (Luke 15:12), meaning he distributed his wealth, his share of the inheritance.
2. More broadly, it refers to everything one possesses and can manage or administer. The younger son received his share and "having gathered all together" he "wasted his goods in prodigal living" (Luke 15:13): he spent entirely what he had received, showing that property is something finite, susceptible to being consumed by folly.
G3776.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "to be" (εἰμί): it literally designates what "is," what exists in its own right, the substance. In common language, it has taken on the meaning of what one possesses in one's own right, what belongs to us, hence "property" and "goods." This root evokes the idea of concrete reality, of what subsists and endures.
G3776.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, exclusively in the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:12-13). In these two occurrences, it designates the inheritance or fortune that the father distributes to his sons and that the younger son subsequently squanders. The context emphasizes the monetary and perishable nature of this good: it can be "gathered" and "wasted," meaning transformed into liquid assets and spent on debauchery. The word thus highlights the fragility of material wealth in the face of poor decisions.
G3776.portee: This parable reminds us that the material goods that God entrusts to us do not belong to us definitively: they can be mismanaged, squandered, or lost. It invites wisdom in the administration of what we possess and acknowledges that all wealth comes from God and can be reclaimed by Him.

sens: Particle that excludes two or more elements simultaneously in a negative enumeration
G3777.detail: 1. It is a negative particle that connects several elements to indicate that none of them exists or occurs. It always functions in pairs (nor…nor) or in series. For example, in Romans 8:38, Paul asserts that "neither death nor life" can separate us from the love of Christ: neither of these two realities has that power. 2. It can also follow another negation (ne, n') to reinforce the exclusion, as in Luke 20:35: "[the resurrected] neither marry nor are given in marriage." The first "ne" already establishes absence; "nor…nor" enumerates the specific cases. 3. Finally, "nor" enumerates impossibilities after a rhetorical question, as in James 3:12: "Can a fig tree produce olives? […] Salt water cannot produce fresh water either"—each "nor" shows what is absurd or contrary to nature.
G3777.origine: This word is a Greek negative particle constructed like a disjunctive negation: it combines the idea of absence (negative root) with an enumeration that isolates each excluded element. In Greek, it resembles other negations like "μή" (mè), but with a distributive nuance: it enumerates what is denied rather than denying it globally. This is why it is particularly useful when multiple cases need to be excluded one by one.
G3777.emploi: The word "nor" (Greek oute) appears 39 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and in Revelation. It is used to exclude physical or moral realities: perishable objects (Matthew 6:20), human relationships (Luke 20:35, 1 Corinthians 11:11), spiritual entities (Romans 8:38-39), spiritual states (Galatians 5:6). Paul uses it frequently to assert that certain differences hold no spiritual significance, or that certain powers cannot reach us. In Acts and the Gospels, he constructs enumerations of impossibilities or logical exclusions: a fig tree does not bear olives (James 3:12), Christ will not be abandoned (Acts 2:31).
G3777.portee: This word reminds the believer of the power of a well-constructed negative assertion. When Paul enumerates what "nor" will separate us from God, he does not simply say "nothing will separate us," but he lists everything that might seem most formidable (death, life, angels, powers…) to better show that none of these obstacles stand. It is an act of faith expressed through systematic exclusion: by rejecting false threats one by one, the believer asserts himself in assurance. This word also helps to see how Scripture structures reasoning: through enumeration and distinction, it teaches to think clearly.

sens: which is here, near the one speaking
the person or thing just mentioned
the person or thing about to be mentioned
used as a verb to be in an explanatory sentence
G3778.detail:
1. This demonstrative primarily designates what is close, visible, present before the eyes: "this man" in Mark 15:39, where the centurion, facing the dying Jesus, exclaims, "this man was the Son of God" — he points to the one he sees.
2. It can also recall what has just been mentioned, as a sort of "you see, this is what I was talking about." In Matthew 5:19, "whoever observes these commandments" refers to the words Jesus has just spoken.
3. Sometimes it announces what will follow: in John 19:36, "these things happened so that the Scripture would be fulfilled" — the word "these" points to the prophetic citation that follows.
4. In Greek, this word can also replace the verb to be: in Matthew 27:46, "τοῦτ᾽ ἐστιν" literally means "this is" and is translated as the explanation "this means."
G3778.origine: This Greek word comes from an archaic root (ὁ-) and is the most common pronunciation for "this" in New Testament Greek. It contrasts with ἐκεῖνος ("that...there, that one"), which is distant or prior: ὗτος points to the present and the near, while ἐκεῖνος evokes what is absent or past. In the Greek Old Testament, this word primarily translates זֶה and זֹאת, the Hebrew demonstratives "this, that."
G3778.emploi: This word is the most frequent in the New Testament — over 1,200 occurrences. It is found everywhere, in all books and contexts. It plays three main roles: first to show ("this Son of God," "this woman"), then to recall what has just been said (epanalepse), or to announce what is to come (prolepse). Sometimes it also expresses a judgment: in Matthew 13:55-56, people ask doubtfully, "from where does this wisdom come?", "who are these sisters?" — the tone can become contemptuous, questioning, or admiring depending on the context.
G3778.portee: This simple yet omnipresent word reminds us that the Christian faith speaks of the concrete and the visible. Jesus is not a distant abstraction: he is "this Son of God" whom the centurion saw die, "this resurrection" of which the apostles are witnesses, "this day of Judgment" that is coming. The Bible constantly connects the present to the past and the future, teaching us to see in Jesus the key to the entire history of salvation.

sens: in this way, in this manner
as it has just been said or described
similarly, likewise
to introduce what follows, what will be stated
with a similar intensity, to that extent
G3779.detail:
1. The word designates the manner in which something is done or happens: "How does this man speak thus?" ask the scribes upon seeing Jesus forgive sins (Mark 2:7). It is the image of the concrete way one acts or expresses oneself.

2. It refers back to what has just been recounted or affirmed to make an application or conclusion: after speaking of the flowers of the field that are clothed without working, Jesus concludes, "thus" God will clothe his children even more (Matthew 6:30). The word "thus" refers to the given example.

3. It expresses a resemblance or equality between two cases: "Likewise, the Lord has commanded those who preach the Gospel to live by the Gospel" (1 Corinthians 9:14). Here the word establishes a parallel.

4. It announces what will follow, as an introductory formula: "Here is what was written by the prophet" (Matthew 2:5) where "here" (the same word in Greek) prepares the reader for an important citation.

5. Used before an adjective or adverb, it marks intensity, the strength of the trait: a shock "so violent" that no house can stand (Revelation 16:18), in other words, "to that extreme extent."
G3779.origine: The word comes from the demonstrative οὗτος (this, that, this one), of which it is the corresponding adverb. It literally means "according to this" or "in this way." It is a very natural formation in the Greek language: from the demonstrative pronoun, the adverb of manner is derived. In Hebrew, the word כֵּן (kèn, "thus") has the same function, and the Greek translators of the New Testament regularly use οὕτως to render it.
G3779.emploi: The word appears 208 times in the New Testament, making it one of the most frequent adverbs if we counted its usages. It is particularly abundant in the Gospel of Matthew and the Gospel of John. It serves several functions: it can refer back to what precedes ("You see? Thus do the disciples"), announce what follows ("Here is how it will be"), establish parallels or comparisons ("Just as... thus also"), or emphasize the intensity of a situation ("so great, so terrible"). In the words of Jesus, it often structures the teaching by linking images to conclusions: after a parable, "thus it will be" introduces the spiritual application.
G3779.portee: For the Christian reader, this small word is a guide to understanding: it signals passages where the Bible draws a lesson, establishes a comparison, or gives instruction. When reading "thus," one knows to connect what precedes with what follows, or to see in an example a truth applicable to one's own life. It is also a word of clarity: it says "here is how things are," inviting the believer to accept reality as God establishes it.

sens: simple negation adverb, which denies an affirmation or fact
reinforced negation, marking a categorical refusal or insistence
in a question, calling for an affirmative response ("isn't it?")
expression of astonishment or protest at what seems obvious
G3780.detail:
1. This is the most common negation in Greek: it simply says "no" to an affirmation. Example: Luke 1:60, Elizabeth refuses the proposed name for her son with a clear "no": "His name will be John."

2. Used for a stronger refusal or condemnation, it insists more than simple negation. In Luke 23:39, the criminal taunts Christ: "Aren't you the Christ?" — a question loaded with sarcasm and mockery.

3. Most of the time, this word poses a rhetorical question: something is asked to force the interlocutor to say "yes." Matthew 5:46: "If you love those who love you, what reward do you deserve? Do not tax collectors do the same?" The expected answer is: "Yes, of course!"

4. Sometimes it expresses indignation at the obviousness of a truth. In Acts 5:4, Peter questions Ananias with a series of insistently asked "no": "Was it not yours alone?" — to push him to confess his lie to God.
G3780.origine: It is a reinforced form of the simple "ou" (basic negation in Greek). The final "chi" (ἵ) gives this word a more marked force, as if emphasizing the refusal. In ancient Hebrew, the negation "lô" played a similar role. This word does not come from a complex etymological root: it is rather an intensified variant, forged to give more weight to the negation, especially in questions and emphatic refusals.
G3780.emploi: This word appears 52 times in the New Testament, especially in the Gospels (Matthew, Luke, John) and in Paul's Epistles. Generally, it poses rhetorical questions to which an affirmative response is implied: "Is it not necessary...?" (Luke 14:28), "Is it not...?" (1 Corinthians 5:12). Sometimes it formulates a clear refusal: Luke 1:60 (refusal of a name), Luke 13:3-5 (one must repent or perish). Paul uses it for his logical arguments: "Has God not given us...?" (Romans 8:32). The context determines whether it is a real question, a denied affirmation, or a protest: the tone of the speaker is as important as the word itself.
G3780.portee: This word teaches how biblical authors argue and persuade: through rhetorical questioning, which forces the reader to respond and reflect. It invites one not to remain passive in the face of the words of Jesus or Paul, but to engage in the dialogue. It also shows that the Bible does not shy away from insistence and emphasis when defending a truth: the reinforced negation is a sign that something truly matters.

sens: One who owes money to someone
One who is obligated to someone by a moral or spiritual debt
One who has committed an offense and must make restitution
One who has an obligation of gratitude towards others
In a spiritual sense, the sinner who must account to God
G3781.detail:
1. A debtor is primarily someone who has borrowed money and must repay it: this is the simplest and most concrete meaning. Matthew 18:24 speaks of a servant who "owed ten thousand talents" — an enormous sum — and could not pay.
2. But the term extends to all kinds of moral debt: someone who has received a benefit is "indebted" to the one who did it and must show gratitude. Paul says in Romans 1:14 that he "owes" the Greeks and the barbarians, meaning he has an obligation to them because he has received the Gospel.
3. It also refers to one who has offended another and must compensate: in Matthew 6:12, we ask God to forgive us our offenses "as we also forgive those who have offended us," these being the debtors of our forgiveness.
4. Generally, a debtor is one who has an obligation to someone — moral, spiritual, or personal — and cannot evade it. Romans 8:12 states that we are not "indebted" to the flesh, meaning we have no obligation to our carnal desires.
5. In a very serious sense, the sinner is a "debtor" to God: he has violated His law and must give an account. In Luke 13:4, those who died in the tower of Siloam are not "more guilty" than others — they do not owe God any more than anyone else — suggesting that every sinner owes something to God.
G3781.origine: The word comes from the verb ὀφείλω (opheilō), which means "to owe" in the sense of financial debt or obligation. Its root image is that of something carried, something that weighs upon oneself. In Hebrew, the word חַיָּב (ḥayāv) expresses the same idea: to be guilty is to be indebted to the law. Thus, Greek and Hebrew converge on a profound understanding: one who has sinned cannot remain neutral; something weighs upon him that must be settled.
G3781.emploi: The word appears in the New Testament to describe very varied situations. First literal: a servant owes money (Matthew 18:24). Then moral and spiritual: Paul explains that he owes the Gospel to different peoples (Romans 1:14), that we owe nothing to our carnal desires (Romans 8:12), that we owe material help to those who have helped us spiritually (Romans 15:27). In the context of prayer, "those who have offended us" are our debtors of forgiveness (Matthew 6:12). Finally, theologically, the word designates the status of the sinner before God — guilty, indebted — and that is why we pray every day to be forgiven our spiritual debt.
G3781.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian life is structured by debts and obligations: to God first (we owe Him everything), to our brothers in Christ (we owe them love and mutual aid), to all men (we owe them the Gospel). It also teaches that forgiveness not only erases a past fault — it frees from the debt, from the weight that crushes. Understanding that we are "debtors" to someone pushes us towards humility, gratitude, and just action.

sens: a sum of money that one must repay to someone
what one is obligated to give or do towards someone
moral or marital obligation
G3782.detail:
1. In its primary sense, a debt is a sum of money that a person must repay to another: it is a concrete financial obligation. Jesus, in the parable of the unforgiving servant (Matthew 18:32), speaks of a servant who owes an enormous sum to his king — a "debt" that he can never repay on his own.
2. The term extends to everything one "owes" morally to someone: respect, honor, taxes, what is rightfully due. Paul, in Romans 13:7, enumerates these various social and civil debts that we must fulfill towards authorities and people in general — taxes, tribute, fear, honor.
3. In marriage, the "debt" refers to the marital obligation: what one spouse "owes" to their partner and vice versa (1 Corinthians 7:3). It is the duty that arises from the marital bond, here the physical intimacy that each owes to the other.
G3782.origine: The word comes from the verb ὀφείλω ("to owe", "to be indebted"), which expresses an obligation — whether financial, moral, or legal. This root is found in other terms related to guilt and obligation. The underlying image is that of a weight one carries: one "owes" something like a burden that cannot be ignored.
G3782.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament (Matthew, Romans, 1 Corinthians), but in very revealing contexts. In Matthew, it refers to a true debt of money — enormous, unpayable — which illustrates divine forgiveness. In Paul, the term shifts from the economic order (taxes) to the moral and marital order, showing that "owing" something goes far beyond money: it is to accept the obligation towards the other that every social or intimate bond creates.
G3782.portee: This word reminds the Christian that he has obligations towards God and others — not just money, but respect, honor, kindness. It also invites gratitude: when one realizes that one cannot pay their own spiritual debt to God, one better understands the grace received. Finally, by recalling marital debts, it emphasizes that Christian love is not a matter of vague sentiment, but a real and mutual commitment.

sens: what one owes to someone, what is due
the wage or payment one deserves
sin considered as an obligation towards God
G3783.detail:
1. A debt is literally something that one owes to someone — an obligation to repay what one has received. In Romans 4:4, Paul uses it to refer to the wage of the worker: what is "due" to him by virtue of his labor, what he has earned through his effort.
2. When it comes to the payment for work, it is a neutral term: it is simply what one justly owes. Paul thus emphasizes that God's grace differs from wages: God does not pay us according to our merits, but gives us freely the gift of salvation.
3. Jesus uses this word strikingly in Matthew 6:12 to speak of sin: "forgive us our offenses." The image is powerful: sin is a debt to God, something we have contracted and cannot repay ourselves. Only forgiveness can free us from it, just as only a creditor can cancel a debt.
G3783.origine: This word comes from the verb "to owe" (ὀφείλω). It is related to Greek terms that express obligation and responsibility. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew/Aramaic חוֹב ("debt"). The word thus primarily designates what one must repay, and by extension any form of duty or obligation that cannot be avoided.
G3783.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Greek New Testament. In Romans 4:4, it is a technical term of commerce: the wage that the worker has earned. In Matthew 6:12, Jesus uses it boldly and metaphorically: sin becomes a "debt" to God. This image was already present in Aramaic texts where "debts" of sin were spoken of. It struck the imagination: one could not repay a debt to God by one's own strength. That is why Jesus teaches us to ask for forgiveness, not payment.
G3783.portee: This image of debt transforms the understanding of sin and forgiveness. Sin is not just a moral stain or an abstract transgression: it is a concrete obligation to God that we have contracted and cannot extinguish by ourselves. It also shows that Christian forgiveness is not sentimental: it is the cancellation of a real debt. When Jesus asks His disciples to "forgive those who have offended us" (Matthew 6:12), He invites them to replicate the act of grace that God has accomplished towards us in Christ.

sens: To be indebted to someone for a sum of money
To be morally or by rule obligated to do something
To be compelled by logic, reason, or propriety
To be required to render a service or a good received
G3784.detail:
1. To owe a sum of money, to be a debtor: in the concrete and financial sense, it means having incurred a debt. The parable in Matthew 18 clearly illustrates this: the servant owes a hundred denarii to his fellow servant (Matthew 18:28), as in the example of the creditor who had two debtors, one owed five hundred denarii and the other fifty (Luke 7:41).

2. To be obliged to do something, to be bound to it: this is a moral or spiritual obligation. Jesus tells his disciples: "you also must wash one another's feet" (John 13:14), meaning it is an act they are required to perform. This is also the case in "we must always give thanks to God" (2 Thessalonians 2:13).

3. To be logically or appropriately bound to do something: the obligation arises from reason or justice. The woman "must have a sign of authority on her head" (1 Corinthians 11:10), or Paul believes that the Gentiles "must also assist them in material things" since they have shared in spiritual benefits (Romans 15:27).

4. In the Aramaic sense, to be guilty towards someone, to have committed an offense: "forgive us our sins as we forgive those who sin against us" (Luke 11:4) uses this verb to speak of the wrong done to others.
G3784.origine: The word comes from a root that primarily evokes the idea of lack or debt. In Hebrew, the verb נָשָׁה (nashâh) means to lend or to be a creditor, and חוֹב (chov) refers to the debt itself. The Greek ὀφείλω initially has the concrete financial meaning, then extends to any form of obligation or moral responsibility. The family of the word includes ὀφείλημα (offelemâ, the debt or offense) and ὀφέιλέτης (ofeíletès, the debtor).
G3784.emploi: The verb ὀφείλω appears 34 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and in the Gospels. In the literal sense of financial debt, it is mostly found in the parables: Matthew 18 with the parable of the unforgiving servant, and Luke 7 with the creditor and his debtors. But the meaning quickly broadens: Paul constantly uses it to express the moral and spiritual obligations of Christians (owing nothing to anyone except to love one another in Romans 13:8, obligation to financially support teachers in 1 Corinthians 9:10, gratitude in 2 Thessalonians 2:13). Matthew 23 uses it in a moral-spiritual sense: the Pharisees who swear by the altar do not see that they "owe" to the God of whom the altar is a symbol. The meaning also refines in the Aramaic sense: in Luke 11:4, forgive us our sins thus expresses the wrong committed against others. Hebrews uses it to say that Christ "had to be made like his brothers" (Hebrews 2:17).
G3784.portee: This word reveals that the Christian life is based on a chain of obligations — not burdens that crush, but responsibilities grounded in justice and love. To owe means that we do not live alone: we are connected to others by what we have received and by what we have committed. Recognizing what we owe leads to gratitude towards God and to brotherly service, while reminding us of mutual forgiveness in case of shortcomings.

sens: Unrealistic or doubtful wish
Regret about the past
Desire for the future
Irony or veiled reproach
G3785.detail:
1. This word expresses a wish that one knows to be impossible or very unlikely. In 1 Corinthians 4:8, Paul says to the Corinthians "may you reign" while they claim to already reign: it is an ironic way of rebuking them by expressing a wish he doubts will truly come to pass.
2. The word can evoke a regret about what could have been in the past. It is the idea of a desire that cannot be fulfilled because the moment has passed.
3. It also expresses a wish for the future, even when that future seems unlikely or difficult. In Revelation 3:15, Christ says to the church in Laodicea "would that you were either cold or hot": he wishes for them to change, but expresses this wish by emphasizing the seriousness of their current state.
4. The word often carries a nuance of irony or hidden reproach. In Galatians 5:12, "would that they were cut off" concerning those who trouble the church expresses a harsh wish, almost like a disguised curse.
G3785.origine: This word comes from the Greek verb "to owe, to be obligated" (which originally means "to have a debt"). It borrows an ancient form, that of the past, but without the usual prefix of the Greek past. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates Hebrew forms that also express wishes or regrets, such as "would to God" or "who that".
G3785.emploi: The New Testament uses it four times, all in Paul and in Revelation. In 1 Corinthians 4:8, Paul uses it to ironically rebuke the pride of the Corinthians. In 2 Corinthians 11:1, he shows a certain impatience: Paul almost ironically asks to be supported. In Galatians 5:12, it is a firm and harsh wish towards false teachers. In Revelation 3:15, Christ uses it to express his disgust at spiritual lukewarmness. Each time, the wish carries emotional or moral weight: it is never a light wish.
G3785.portee: This word reminds us that true biblical wishes are not passive dreams: they always carry a judgment or a call to change. When Paul or Christ express a "may it be", they do not simply dream — they rebuke, they exhort, they judge. For the reader, it is a lesson: the wishes of the apostles and of Christ are words of weight, charged with authority and love, and never trivial.

sens: What brings profit, what is useful or beneficial for oneself
What serves a purpose, what is effective
Material profit or gain
Spiritual or moral benefit
G3786.detail:
1. Advantage is primarily what benefits us, what brings us profit. Paul asks: "What advantage is it to me?" to fight against beasts in Ephesus, if the dead do not rise (1 Corinthians 15:32) — that is, what is the point of facing danger if I have no ultimate gain, no eternal benefit?
2. The word also designates what "serves", what is useful or effective in achieving a goal. James asks: "What good is it?" to say one has faith without works (James 2:14) — that is, does such faith really benefit us, can it save us? Similarly, offering words of comfort without clothing or food to someone who is hungry, "what good is that?" (James 2:16) — it helps no one, it benefits no one.
G3786.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that means "to increase, to augment". Advantage is therefore what enriches us, what adds to us for our benefit. This simple and concrete term designates any material or moral gain, anything that is beneficial or useful to us.
G3786.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in contexts questioning utility or profit. Paul uses it in his argument about the resurrection: without it, what advantage is there in suffering (1 Corinthians 15:32)? James repeats it twice in the same passage to show that faith without works is useless: it benefits neither the one who claims it nor the one who needs it. It is a word of reproach: it interrogates what yields nothing.
G3786.portee: This word invites the Christian not to be mistaken about what truly profits. Paul and James remind us that some things may seem useful or desirable (pleasure, words without action) but bring no real benefit: they do not save, they do not help. True faith is measured by its concrete fruits. Therefore, the Christian must constantly ask: what does this really profit me? Not in the sense of selfishness, but in the sense of wisdom: seeking true profit, that which lasts, that which also benefits others.

sens: Work done only when being observed
Obedience motivated by the gaze of men rather than by sincerity
Devotion that disappears once not seen
G3787.detail: 1. The word literally refers to a service rendered "under the eye": it is work done only when one knows they are being watched. In Ephesians 6:6 and Colossians 3:22, Paul uses it to warn: a slave should not obey their master "only in their presence", meaning only because they fear their gaze. 2. This is hypocritical obedience, based on the fear of human judgment: one pretends to do well to please the observer, not out of true conviction. 3. By extension, it is a form of superficial and opportunistic devotion: it is abandoned as soon as one is no longer observed, because it does not come from the heart.
G3787.origine: The word is composed of two Greek elements: "ophthalmos" (the eye) and "douleia" (service, slavery). This figurative composition depicts someone who adjusts their behavior to the presence of another's gaze. It is a rare word, likely coined by Paul himself to strike his readers: it appears only twice in the New Testament, in letters addressed to servants.
G3787.emploi: Paul uses this expression only in Ephesians 6:6 and Colossians 3:22, two parallel verses addressed to the servants (slaves) of Christian households. In both cases, he exhorts them to reject this "eye service" in favor of sincere service to the Lord. The context is clear: it is not about ceasing to obey the master according to the flesh, but about changing the motive — moving from the fear of human gaze to the love and fear of God. It is a precise theological term to name a common moral flaw.
G3787.portee: This word highlights a universal temptation: to do good or render service only because one is being observed. Paul invites every believer — slave or free — to cultivate sincere obedience and devotion, motivated by the love of Christ and not by concern for their reputation among men. It is a lesson in inner freedom and authenticity: to act with integrity when no one is watching, because one knows that God always sees.

sens: Organ of sight, allowing one to see
Ability to perceive, to understand
Gaze, attention, intention
Malice, envy, jealousy
Perspective or point of view
Opening, hole or visual mark
G3788.detail:
1. The eye is the physical organ of vision: it is through it that we see the world. Matthew 5:29 speaks of "your right eye", as a part of the body that can see and cause harm. John 9:15 recounts how a blind man regains his sight after washing his eyes where mud had been applied.

2. The eye symbolizes the ability to understand and perceive spiritual truth. Jesus says in Matthew 13:15 that some "have eyes but do not see" — they do not grasp the meaning of the parables or the message of God, even as they look. Ephesians 1:18 prays that "the eyes of your heart" may be enlightened: the eye of the heart is the inner understanding.

3. The eye embodies the gaze, the attention one gives to someone or something. Luke 6:20 says that Jesus "looked up" at his disciples to teach them. It is a gaze that turns toward someone with intention.

4. A "bad eye" signifies envy and jealousy. Matthew 6:22-23 contrasts the "good eye" (generous, loyal) with the "bad eye" (greedy, envious): these are not physical eyes, but moral qualities expressed through the image of the eye.

5. The eye can also express perspective or judgment: being "in someone's eyes" means being judged, estimated by them. Hebrews 4:13 states that everything is "in the eyes of him to whom we must give account" — nothing escapes him.

6. By extension, the eye denotes an opening or visible mark, like that which sight allows to pass through.
G3788.origine: The Greek word ὀφθαλμός comes from a very ancient root denoting the organ of sight. In Hebrew, the equivalent is עַיִן (ayin), which has the same primary meaning and figurative uses. The Greek word retains both the concrete sense (the organ) and metaphorical uses: a "bad eye" in Greek translates the Hebrew expression "bad eye" which means envy. This permanence of figurative language across cultures shows that the Bible speaks to the human heart in a universal way.
G3788.emploi: The word "eye" appears 86 times in the New Testament (mostly in the plural, "eyes"). It is omnipresent in the Gospels to describe both physical healings (John 9 recounts how Jesus heals a blind man), teachings (Matthew 6:22-23 on the good or bad eye), and spiritual blindness (Matthew 13:15, Luke 19:42). Paul uses the expression "eyes of the heart" (Ephesians 1:18) to speak of spiritual understanding. The image of the eye also allows for the expression of God's vigilance (1 Peter 3:12, Hebrews 4:13): nothing escapes him. The word thus constantly oscillates between the physical and spiritual sense, as if the Bible invites the reader to see beyond the visible.
G3788.portee: Understanding the biblical "eye" means recognizing that physical vision and spiritual vision are inseparable. Jesus heals the blind not only to restore their sight but to reveal that only he can truly make us see. The warning about the "bad eye" (envy) invites us to examine our intentions: what comes out of our eyes reflects what resides in our hearts. Finally, the certainty that everything is "in the eyes of God" reminds the Christian that nothing escapes God's judgment and mercy: it is both a warning and a comfort.

sens: Crawling animal with scales, without legs
Cunning and deceptive creature
Figure of prudent and alert wisdom
Symbol of the devil and Satan
Object of curse and divine judgment
G3789.detail:
1. The serpent is a real animal, recognizable by its sinuous shape without limbs: this is the primary sense, shown in Luke 10:19 when Jesus gives his disciples the power to tread on serpents and scorpions.
2. The serpent embodies cunning and deception, as the one who seduced Eve in the Garden of Eden. Paul invokes it in 2 Corinthians 11:3 to warn that the serpent has led believers away from simplicity through its cunning — a very ancient biblical image of intelligent malice.
3. Jesus commands his disciples to be "wise as serpents" (Matthew 10:16), showing that one can borrow from this animal a certain vigilance and discernment, without the malice that often accompanies it.
4. In Revelation 12:9 and 20:2, the serpent designates Satan himself, the devil who deceives the whole earth — this is the most serious spiritual sense of the word in the New Testament.
5. Jesus calls the religious leaders "serpents, brood of vipers" (Matthew 23:33), associating the serpent with judgment and condemnation, for how could they escape the punishment of hell.
G3789.origine: The Greek word ὄφις (ophis) comes from an ancient root that evokes the idea of folding or sinuousness, like the characteristic shape of the reptile. It translates the Hebrew נָחָשׁ (nakash) from the Old Testament, the same word that designates the tempting serpent of the Garden of Eden in Genesis 3. From the beginning, the biblical serpent carries within it a dual nature: ordinary creature and symbol of spiritual cunning.
G3789.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and Revelation. As a real animal, it is found in concrete situations (Matthew 7:10, Mark 16:18). But very quickly, the usage becomes figurative and theological: the serpent of Moses lifted up in the desert (John 3:14) prefigures Christ lifted on the cross; the cunning of the serpent serves as a comparison to describe spiritual seduction (2 Corinthians 11:3); finally, Revelation identifies the serpent with Satan himself, especially in 12:9 and 20:2, thus marking the transition from symbol to the spiritual character that has inhabited it since the beginning.
G3789.portee: For the Christian, the serpent reminds us of two vital warnings: first, the constant threat of cunning and seduction that can lead us away from Christ, as in the Garden of Eden; second, the promised victory over Satan for those who walk in the power given by Jesus. The serpent thus becomes a sign that the spiritual world is real and active, and that trust in Christ alone protects us from the one who "deceives the whole earth."

sens: Bony arch above the eye, the eyebrow or the forehead region
Ridge, highest point of a mountain or hill
G3790.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the brow ridge, the bony part that forms the edge of the eye socket. This is the literal and anatomical meaning of the Greek term.
2. By extension, it evokes the ridge, the highest point of a mountain or hill. Luke 4:29 illustrates this clearly: the inhabitants of Nazareth threaten to throw Jesus from the "summit" of the mountain on which their city was built. The image is that of the highest point, the steep edge from which one risks falling.
G3790.origine: The Greek word ὀφρῦς comes from an ancient root expressing something that overhangs or protrudes. The Hebrew עַיִן־גַב (literally "eyebrow of the eye" or "arch of the eye") is its equivalent in the Old Testament. The same root can refer to both the human eyebrow and any ridge or crest that rises and dominates.
G3790.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 4:29, in the account of the attempted stoning of Jesus in Nazareth. The context reveals that it refers to a dangerously exposed place: the inhabitants want to throw him from the top of a cliff. Although the word could theoretically evoke an eyebrow, its topographical meaning (the ridge of a mountain) is appropriate here. Matthew 13:58 reports the same event without this specific detail.
G3790.portee: This passage shows how Jesus faced violent rejection in his own region. The summit of the mountain symbolizes the hostility of his own people, who wanted to harm him. It reminds Christians that rejection and misunderstanding can come from those closest to us, and that Jesus expected this.

sens: Physically agitate, shake
Disturb someone, unsettle them
Cause suffering, affliction
Be agitated, in a state of turmoil or distress
G3791.detail: 1. The verb ὀχλέω first paints the image of physical agitation, like a movement of a crowd or trouble: to shake or stir something or someone. 2. From there, it means to disturb someone in their peace or calm, to unsettle them in a way that causes discomfort. 3. More strongly, it expresses the idea of tormenting, causing suffering: inflicting an affliction, a burden on the person. This meaning appears in Acts 5:16, where people "tormented by unclean spirits" describes individuals in a state of agitation and suffering caused by these spirits; the word emphasizes the distress and instability they endure. 4. In the passive voice (as in Acts 5:16), the verb can also describe the state of the one who is tormented: being in agitation, anxiety, or inner disturbance.
G3791.origine: The verb ὀχλέω comes from ὄχλος (ochlos), which means "crowd" or "multitude." The etymological link suggests the original idea: being in the midst of an agitated crowd, or being shaken by the noise and turmoil of a crowd. From there, the general meaning of "disturb" or "unsettle" developed. The word belongs to a family of Greek terms expressing agitation and instability.
G3791.emploi: The verb ὀχλέω is used only once in the New Testament, in Acts 5:16 in the passive voice. In this context, Luke describes the crowd pressing toward Jerusalem to bring the sick and "those tormented by unclean spirits" to Peter and the other apostles. The word here denotes not just a simple physical illness, but a spiritual and existential distress: these individuals are agitated, deeply troubled by the presence of unclean spirits within them. The verse illustrates how the verb ὀχλέω, though rare, carries a strong emotional charge, emphasizing active suffering, the turmoil of the soul as well as the body.
G3791.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reveals that evil (here, unclean spirits) does not leave people indifferent or frozen: it torments them, agitates them, puts them in distress. It is a reminder that the power of Jesus and his apostles operates over this very turmoil; the healing announced in Acts 5:16 is liberation from true inner agitation. The word also invites us to recognize the real suffering of those under the power of evil, and therefore to place our hope in God's power to free them.

sens: Sow trouble and agitation in a crowd to provoke disorder
Gather a crowd by exciting them against someone or something
G3792.detail:
1. This verb describes the action of intentionally sowing trouble and confusion among people — spreading agitation like one spreads a trail of powder. In Acts 17:5, the Jews jealous of Paul "spread agitation" in the city by inflaming the spirits, which leads the crowd to gather in front of Jason's house to seek the apostle.
2. The word also evokes the idea of gathering a crowd, but a manipulated crowd, excited, mobilized against a specific goal — not by persuasion, but by stirring up emotions. This is the work of those who know how to play on passions to create disorder.
G3792.origine: The word is composed of two elements: "ochlos" (crowd, multitude) and "poieō" (to make, produce). It literally means "to make a crowd" or "to create disorder with a crowd." The verb appears only once in the New Testament, making it a rather rare expression to qualify a specific act: to intentionally incite a crowd to rise up.
G3792.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament: Acts 17:5, during Paul's stay in Thessalonica. The Jews who reject Paul's message resort to manipulating the crowds to stop him. They do not refute his message through debate, but provoke public disorder by exciting common men. It is a picture of the destructive power of orchestrated agitation: a few jealous leaders can sow chaos throughout an entire city by playing on the feelings of the masses.
G3792.portee: This word exposes how jealousy and rejection of the Gospel can drive some to resort to manipulation and agitation rather than honesty. It also shows the fragility of public peace in the face of those who know how to exploit crowds. For the Christian, it is a warning: we must distinguish legitimate spiritual passion from manipulative agitation, and recognize when the rejection of the Word degenerates into organized violence.

sens: A multitude of people gathered in one place
A large group that moves or acts together
The whole people, the popular mass
Ordinary people, in contrast to authorities or elites
G3793.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a multitude of people, a dense assembly. In Matthew 4:25, "a great crowd followed him" shows thousands of people converging towards Jesus from different regions. It is the crowd as a concrete, tangible reality, often amazed or enthusiastic.
2. The crowd is also a group in motion: in Mark 5:27, the woman with a bleeding issue comes "in the crowd" and presses in, showing people in contact with one another, circulating around Jesus. It is the crowd as a collective dynamic.
3. In Luke 3:7, John the Baptist addresses "those who came in crowds to be baptized," which designates the whole people as a whole, without distinction of rank. The crowd becomes synonymous with the people themselves.
4. Finally, the crowd often represents ordinary people, popular opinion, in contrast to leaders and scholars. In Mark 12:37, Mark notes that "the crowd" (the opinion of the people) listened to Jesus with pleasure, while the authorities opposed him.
G3793.origine: The Greek word ὄχλος (ochlos) originally evokes a moving mass, almost chaotic. It corresponds in Hebrew to הָמוֹן (hamon, tumult, noise of a crowd) and to קָהָל (qahal, assembly). Unlike δῆμος (demos, the people as an organized political entity), ὄχλος emphasizes the spontaneous and disorganized nature of the multitude. This is why Roman and Jewish authorities often viewed the crowd with suspicion: it was not a structured political body, but a mass capable of being stirred up quickly.
G3793.emploi: The word appears 171 times in the New Testament, especially in the Gospels. It is very frequent in Matthew, Mark, and Luke, who describe Jesus' activity in relation to the crowds. The crowds come to him (Matthew 4:25), touch him (Mark 5:27), receive his teaching (Matthew 13:2, Mark 4:1), follow him (Luke 3:7), and sometimes defend him (Matthew 21:46, Mark 11:32). The context shows that Jesus viewed the crowd with compassion (Matthew 9:36, Mark 6:34), while the scribes and Pharisees sought to influence it against him (Matthew 27:20). The crowd is sometimes enthusiastic and grateful, sometimes manipulated or fickle.
G3793.portee: The crowd in the Gospels teaches us that Jesus did not teach and work only for an elite, but for the whole people, for all who come to him. It also reminds us of our own responsibility: we are called not only to follow Jesus individually but to share his word with others, not allowing the opinion of the moment to divert us from the truth. The crowd also illustrates how the masses can be both receptive to the Spirit and fragile in the face of the pressures of authorities.

sens: Fortified military construction, place of defense
Figuratively: that in which one places their trust, what seems to protect us
G3794.detail: 1. A fortress is a fortified structure, a military defense place — a location surrounded by thick walls where one takes refuge to resist the enemy. It is an image of strength and security. 2. Figuratively, the Bible uses this word to designate anything in which people place their trust and believe they are protected: ideas, arguments, false certainties that barricade us against the truth of God. In 2 Corinthians 10:4, Paul speaks of the mental "fortresses" that bad reasoning raises against God — thoughts that believe themselves impregnable but which the power of God can overthrow.
G3794.origine: The word comes from the verb ὀχυρόω (to fortify, to make solid), itself based on ὀχυρός (strong, sturdy). The root evokes the idea of solidity and protection. In Hebrew, the word מִבְצָר (mibtsar) referred to both military fortresses and refuges; Greek takes up this duality: the concrete meaning of a defensive construction and the spiritual meaning of what "protects" us against the word of God.
G3794.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 10:4. Paul uses it in the context of his apostolic ministry: he asserts that his weapons are not carnal (swords, spears) but spiritual — the word of God and prayer — and that they are capable of overthrowing the mental fortresses of unbelief and rebellion against God. This passage transposes the traditional military image into the spiritual and psychological realm: it is not stone ramparts that are fought against, but citadels of pride and false wisdom.
G3794.portee: This word reminds Christians that true battles are not fought on a physical or material level, but on the level of thoughts and convictions. It invites us to recognize and dismantle the "fortresses" we build — unbiblical certainties, prejudices, fears — to submit them to the authority of Christ. It is a call to spiritual vigilance and to trust in the power of God rather than in our own defenses.

sens: Small fish or portion of fish prepared for consumption
Food made from fish, serving as a relish or accompaniment to bread
Food that Jesus uses in the miracles of feeding and meals
G3795.detail:
1. The word ὀψάριον is a diminutive: it refers to a small fish or a portion of fish, often prepared or cooked. In John 6:9, the young boy brings "two fish" alongside five barley loaves — modest portions intended for a simple meal.

2. This word also expresses the idea of a relish or accompaniment, a kind of delicacy eaten with bread. It is a choice food, not ordinary. In John 6:11, after Jesus had given thanks, he also distributes fish "as much as they wanted" — a generosity that contrasts with the initial scarcity.

3. In the accounts of John, fish plays a role in the moments when Jesus feeds his disciples or the crowd. In John 21:9-13, after the resurrection, on the shore of the lake, there is bread and fish on a charcoal fire, and Jesus gives them to eat — an image of communion and abundance.
G3795.origine: The word ὀψάριον is a diminutive of ὄψον, which means "prepared dish," "relish," or "fish" (the quintessential cooked food). This root evokes a dish accompanying bread, a complementary food that garnishes the meal. The diminutive emphasizes the modest aspect or the reduced portion. The word appears only in the New Testament (John), it is a term from late Greek and spoken language.
G3795.emploi: ὀψάριον appears 5 times, exclusively in the Gospel of John: twice in chapter 6 (the miracle of the multiplication of the loaves), three times in chapter 21 (the meal of the resurrected one by the lake). In John 6, it refers to the two small fish of the young boy, which became food for the crowd — an act of divine power. In John 21, the fish is on the coals, ready to be shared, symbolizing the provision of the resurrected Jesus. The word remains always a concrete food, never abstract or symbolic in its use.
G3795.portee: The fish reminds us that Jesus, through his power, nourishes and provides for the concrete needs of those who follow him. It is also a symbol of communion: in the two major contexts (multiplication and meal of the resurrected), the sharing of fish unites the community around Jesus. These images invite the believer to recognize their dependence on Christ and to live in trust concerning their daily needs.

sens: The time of day when the sun sets, when light declines
Late in the day, towards the end of the day
After, once passed (referring to time)
G3796.detail: 1. Ὀψέ primarily refers to the evening, the moment when daylight fades and shadows lengthen. Mark 11:19 uses it this way: "When evening came, Jesus went out of the city" — it is the hour when work stops and night begins. 2. The word can also mean "late," that is, late in the day, enumerating different times: Mark 13:35 states, "in the evening, or at midnight, or at the crowing of the rooster, or in the morning," placing evening among the nocturnal or twilight hours. 3. In later contexts of written Greek, ὀψέ can mean "after," indicating that something occurs once a moment or period has passed. Matthew 28:1 uses it this way: "After the Sabbath, at dawn on the first day," where ὀψέ marks that the action follows the end of the Sabbath rest.
G3796.origine: Ὀψέ comes from a root that denotes what is late or delayed in time. In Hebrew, the Old Testament speaks of evening with עֶרֶב ("erev"), which is particularly found in descriptions of times of day or sacrifices offered "between the two evenings." The Greek word has the appearance of a simple and direct adverb, serving to situate an action in time rather than to describe it.
G3796.emploi: Ὀψέ appears three times in the Gospels according to the provided usages. Mark uses it twice to speak of evening as a concrete moment of the day: in verse 11:19 to indicate when Jesus left Jerusalem, in verse 13:35 to enumerate the hours when the Lord may come. Matthew 28:1 uses it differently, no longer to designate a moment of the day but to mean "after": it marks that the resurrection manifests after the Sabbath is completed. This shift in meaning shows how the late Greek of the New Testament uses this small word to situate events in time, whether it concerns the hour of the day or the order of events.
G3796.portee: For the believer, evening reminds us that Jesus continues His work at the moment we rest. Mark 11:19 shows that in the evening, when the city sleeps, Jesus is still at work. Mark 13:35 urges us to be vigilant at all times, including when we would be sleeping. And Matthew 28:1 announces hope: after death and the Sabbath rest comes the resurrection — after every night comes a new morning.

sens: The rain that falls late in the season, after the autumn rains
Figuratively, what happens late in a process of waiting or maturation
G3797.detail:
1. In Palestine, the rain cycle is crucial for crops. Rain comes in two phases: first the early rains in autumn (October-November), then the late or latter rains at the end of winter and the beginning of spring (March-April). The latter is essential for grains to mature before harvest. The word opsimos specifically denotes this second series of rains, which occurs "late" in the agricultural season. In James 5:7, the farmer "waits for the precious fruit of the earth" by receiving successively "the early and the latter rains" — he depends on this natural rhythm for his harvest.
2. The image of the late rain also symbolizes what comes after a long wait, completing a process that has been long underway. Just as the farmer patiently waits to receive the last rain that will allow the harvest, the believer can patiently await the fulfillment of God's promises, knowing that the final moment will come.
G3797.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective opsé ("late, delayed"), which expresses the idea of something occurring late in time or in a sequence. In the Greek Old Testament, opsimos primarily translates the Hebrew malkosh (מַלְקוֹשׁ), a technical term for the late rain in Palestine. It is a poetic and late word, uncommon in classical Greek.
G3797.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in James 5:7. The apostle James uses it to exhort believers to patience: they must wait for the coming of the Lord as a farmer waits for the two cycles of rain essential for his harvest. This agricultural and Palestinian context makes the image very concrete for the original readers, who were well acquainted with this reality of climate and farming. The word emphasizes the importance of patient waiting until the final moment when what is expected arrives.
G3797.portee: This image speaks directly to the believer: the Christian life resembles the work of the farmer, a succession of periods where one must wait patiently, without haste. Just as both rains are necessary for the harvest, the trials and waiting times of the believer contribute to their spiritual maturation. James reminds us that patience is not resigned inaction, but active trust: we know that the "final rain" will come, and that the precious fruit will eventually arrive.

sens: the time of day when the sun sets, between day and night
the meal taken at the end of the day
to consider, examine (rare sense)
G3798.detail:
1. Evening is the time of day when light fades and night approaches. It is the hour when people finish their work and gather together. In the Gospel accounts, Jesus heals the sick in the evening (Matthew 8:16), teaches His disciples at the table in the evening (Matthew 26:20), and dies in the afternoon, just before evening falls (Mark 15:42: "when evening came").
2. By extension, the word also refers to the evening meal, the time when people gather around the table. When "evening came," the master of the vineyard pays his workers (Matthew 20:8), as if it were the hour to close the work and settle accounts.
3. In a very rare usage (Mark 11:11), the related verb means "to consider, to look at": Jesus "considers" the temple before leaving, as if He were examining it carefully.
G3798.origine: The Greek word ὀψία (opsia) comes from the root ὀψέ (opsé), which means "late, tardy." It is a substantivized adjective: literally "the late hour." The root evokes the idea of what comes last, after the day. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, this word often renders the Hebrew עֶרֶב (erev), which denotes both evening and the onset of night.
G3798.emploi: The word appears 15 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in Matthew (7 times) and Mark (7 times), and twice in John. It is a very concrete term, rooted in daily life: it marks key moments in the story of Jesus. In the evening, Jesus heals (Matthew 8:16, Mark 1:32), prays alone (Matthew 14:23), teaches His disciples (Matthew 26:20, Mark 14:17), crosses the lake (Mark 4:35, John 6:16), and dies (Mark 15:42). Evening is the hour of transition, rest, and often miracle. The rare usage of the verb (Mark 11:11) shows that the word can also mean "to examine" or "to observe," as if one were "looking" attentively.
G3798.portee: Evening in the Gospels is never a mere detail of the setting: it is the hour when Jesus performs His mighty acts, where He withdraws to pray, where He shares intimacy with His disciples. This emphasis on evening invites the reader to see that the Lord is present in all times of the day, and that the fatigue of the day does not halt His action. Recognizing evening as a blessed moment of encounter with God can transform our own experience of the day that ends.

sens: The act of seeing, sight
The face, the countenance, the features of the face
The outward appearance, what is visible
G3799.detail:
1. The primary meaning is the act or ability to see, the visual faculty itself — it is not the sight of a particular thing, but the power to see in general.

2. The face or countenance: this is what is seen first in a person, their features, their expression. When the risen Lord appears in Revelation, John describes His face as shining like the sun in its strength (Revelation 1:16); when Lazarus comes out of the tomb, his face is wrapped in a cloth (John 11:44).

3. The outward appearance or what is apparent to the eyes: this is what is judged first, before knowing the deeper reality. Jesus rebukes those who judge "according to appearance" by saying: "Do not judge according to appearance, but judge with righteous judgment" (John 7:24) — we must look beyond what we see.
G3799.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to see." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the word marèh (מַרְאֶה) was primarily used to refer to what is seen, the appearance or the vision. The Greek opsis retains this idea of what falls under the gaze.
G3799.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament. It first refers to the concrete face of individuals: that of the resurrected Lazarus (John 11:44) and that of the glorified Christ (Revelation 1:16), with an emphasis on His beauty or supernatural aspect. But Jesus also uses it in the sense of "appearance" to urge not to remain on the surface of things: to judge according to appearance is to stop at what is seen without seeking the deeper truth (John 7:24). The word thus encompasses both the physical face and what is presented at first glance.
G3799.portee: This word reminds us that the face is the most visible part of ourselves, the part that touches others at first glance. But it warns us: Jesus calls us to go beyond appearance, not to judge based on what we see. It is an invitation to depth in our relationships with others and in understanding the truth.

sens: The ripe fruit of the tree, at harvest time in late summer
Figuratively: the desires and pleasures of the earthly world
G3703.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the ripe fruit that is harvested, particularly in late summer and early autumn. This is the time when the tree produces its finished product, ready to be eaten. In Revelation 18:14, John speaks of the "fruits" that Babylon desired — the luxury goods and wealth that it loved to consume.
2. Figuratively, "fruit" symbolizes the material desires and pleasures sought by a world without God. The image is that of the tasty fruit that one loves to savor: the delicate, magnificent, and attractive things. In the same verse, all these fruits, all these pleasures, disappear forever — an image of the vanity of everything that is not eternal.
G3703.origine: The Greek word ὀπώρα comes from a root that designates the season of harvest, the time when the fruits reach maturity. It refers to a natural cycle: growth leads to the moment when the fruit is ready. It is a concrete word that draws its imagery from agriculture and rural life.
G3703.emploi: The word appears only once in Revelation 18:14 (Segond 1910). John uses it to speak of the luxuries and riches that Babylon — the great city under judgment — loved to possess and enjoy. "The fruits that your soul desired" refers to precious goods, the products of the earth and human labor, all the pleasures that can be eaten or owned. The term emphasizes that these are material, concrete, desirable things — but perishable and destined to disappear in God's judgment.
G3703.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the true nature of pleasure and material wealth. The "fruits" that seem so tasty, so attractive, so lasting, are only so for a moment. Those who build their lives on these desires will discover, too late, that they have pursued things that vanish. The Christian is called not to set their heart on the productions of the world, but to seek what lasts forever.
